Marked points on translation surfaces

Paul Apisa and Alex Wright
Abstract.

We show that all G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) equivariant point markings over orbit closures of translation surfaces arise from branched covering constructions and periodic points, completely classify such point markings over strata of quadratic differentials, and give applications to the finite blocking problem.

1. Introduction

In this paper, we give new results on the G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) action on moduli spaces of translation surfaces with marked points, and applications such as the following.

The finite blocking problem. We say that two, not necessarily distinct, points x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} on a rational polygon are finitely blocked if there is a finite set BB of points such that every billiard trajectory from x1x_{1} to x2x_{2} passes through a point of BB. We call a polygon Gaussian if it can be tiled by isometric (π4,π4,π2)(\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{2}) triangles in such a way that triangles with overlapping edges are related via reflection in that edge. Similarly we call it rectangle-tiled if it can be tiled by rectangles and Eisenstein if it can be tiled by (π6,π3,π2)(\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{2}) triangles. We adopt the convention that all polygons are required to have connected boundary and do not have slits.

Theorem 1.1.

Let PP be a rational polygon.

  1. (1)

    If PP is Gaussian, Eisenstein, or rectangle-tiled, then any two points are finitely blocked.

  2. (2)

    If PP is not Gaussian, Eisenstein, or rectangle-tiled and all its angles are multiples of π/2\pi/2, then possibly infinitely many pairs of points are finitely blocked, but each point is finitely blocked from only finitely many other points.

  3. (3)

    Otherwise, only finitely many pairs of points are finitely blocked in PP.

The main content is the third statement; the first two are included for completeness and are closely related to previous results (see for example Theorems 1 and 2 of Lelièvre, Monteil, Weiss [LMW16]). We prove Theorem 1.1 by showing that every translation surface that is not a branched cover of a torus has a finite set that, together with covering maps to half-translation surfaces, accounts for all finite blocking (see Theorems 3.6 and 3.16). Theorem 1.1 builds upon and recovers results of authors such as Gutkin, Hubert, Lelièvre, Monteil, Schmidt, Schmoll, Troubetzkoy, and Weiss, which we will discuss shortly. Our results also apply to the illumination problem, which is the special case of the finite blocking problem when the blocking set is required to be empty.

Affine invariant submanifolds. Given a partition of 2​g−22g-2 as a sum of positive integers 2​g−2=∑i=1ski2g-2=\sum_{i=1}^{s}k_{i}, define the stratum ℋ⁡(k1,…,ks)\mathcal{H}(k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}) to be the orbifold of all translation surfaces (X,ω)(X,\omega) where XX has genus gg and ω\omega has zeros of order k1,…,ksk_{1},\ldots,k_{s}. A result of Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi [EM18, EMM15] gives that any closed G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) invariant subset of a stratum is an affine invariant submanifold, which is by definition a properly immersed smooth orbifold whose image is locally described by real homogeneous linear equations in period coordinates.

Marked points on translation surfaces. Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be an affine invariant submanifold of a stratum ℋ\mathcal{H} of translation surfaces. Let ℋ∗n\mathcal{H}^{*n} denote the set of surfaces in ℋ\mathcal{H} with nn distinct marked points, none of which coincide with each other or with zeros of the Abelian differential. Let π:ℋ∗n→ℋ\pi:\mathcal{H}^{*n}\to\mathcal{H} be the map that forgets the marked points.

Define an nn-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M} to be an affine invariant submanifold 𝒩\mathcal{N} of ℋ∗n\mathcal{H}^{*n} such that π⁡(𝒩)\pi(\mathcal{N}) is equal to a dense subset of ℳ\mathcal{M} (equivalently, π⁡(𝒩)\pi(\mathcal{N}) contains ℳ\mathcal{M} minus a finite, possibly empty, union of smaller dimensional affine invariant submanifolds). Define an ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point to be a 11-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M} of the same dimension as ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Theorem 1.2 (Eskin-Filip-Wright).

An affine invariant submanifold has infinitely many periodic points if and only if it consists entirely of branched covers of tori.

Section 4.2 explains why Theorem 1.2 is a special case of results in [EFW18].

If ℳ\mathcal{M} is a closed orbit containing (X,ω)(X,\omega), the ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points correspond to finite orbits of the affine symmetry group on (X,ω)(X,\omega). As we will discuss, in this case Theorem 1.2 was previously known [GHS03, Möl06].

An easy example of periodic points is provided by Weierstrass points whenever ℳ\mathcal{M} consists of hyperelliptic surfaces.

Given an n′n^{\prime}-point marking 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} over ℳ\mathcal{M}, and an n′′n^{\prime\prime}-point marking 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} over ℳ\mathcal{M}, we will say that any irreducible component of

{(X,ω,S′∪S′′):(X,ω,S′)∈𝒩′,(X,ω,S′′)∈𝒩′′,|S1∪S2|=n′+n′′}\{(X,\omega,S^{\prime}\cup S^{\prime\prime}):(X,\omega,S^{\prime})\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime},(X,\omega,S^{\prime\prime})\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime},|S_{1}\cup S_{2}|=n^{\prime}+n^{\prime\prime}\}

is a fiberwise union of 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} and 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime}. One defines a fiberwise union of more than two point markings in the same way.

We say that an nn-point marking 𝒩\mathcal{N} over ℳ\mathcal{M} is reducible if it is a fiberwise union of other point markings. We call a point marking irreducible if it is not reducible.

Every point marking is a fiberwise union of irreducible point markings, which we call its irreducible pieces. In this way, the study of point markings immediately reduces to the irreducible case.

The following result states that when ℳ\mathcal{M} does not consist entirely of torus covers the only non-obvious ways to mark points over ℳ\mathcal{M} are to mark ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points. This result arose during conversations with Ronen Mukamel.

Theorem 1.3.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be an affine invariant submanifold that does not consist entirely of branched covers of tori. Any irreducible nn-point marking 𝒩\mathcal{N} over ℳ\mathcal{M} with n>1n>1 arises from a half-translation surface covering construction: for any (X,ω,S)∈𝒩(X,\omega,S)\in\mathcal{N}, there is a translation covering map from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to a half-translation surface that takes SS to a single point.

A translation covering map from a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) to a quadratic differential (Q,q)(Q,q) is defined to be a branched covering f:X→Qf:X\to Q of Riemann surfaces such that ω2=f∗​(q)\omega^{2}=f^{*}(q). A Riemann surface with a non-zero quadratic differential is also called a half-translation surface.

Theorem 1.3 implies a stronger statement, which we allude to with the terminology “covering construction”. See Remark 3.5. In the case that ℳ\mathcal{M} does consist entirely of branched covers of tori, point markings are easily described, and there are infinitely many irreducible nn-point markings for all n≥1n\geq 1.

Strata of quadratic differentials. For any connected component of a stratum 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of quadratic differentials, one can form the affine invariant submanifold 𝒬~\tilde{\mathcal{Q}} consisting of all Abelian differentials which arise as double covers (also called square roots) of quadratic differentials in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Each (X,ω)∈𝒬~(X,\omega)\in\tilde{\mathcal{Q}} has a natural involution JJ, so that (X/J,ω2)∈𝒬(X/J,\omega^{2})\in\mathcal{Q}. (Since (X,ω)(X,\omega) might, in unusual cases, have more than one involution, the data of JJ should be included in a point of 𝒬~\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}, but rather than write (X,ω,J)∈𝒬~(X,\omega,J)\in\tilde{\mathcal{Q}} we suppress this from the notation.)

If 𝒬\mathcal{Q} consists entirely of hyperelliptic surfaces we say that 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is hyperelliptic. In this case the hyperelliptic involution on X/JX/J lifts to a hyperelliptic involution on XX.

Theorem 1.4.

Suppose 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), 𝒬⁡(2,−12)\mathcal{Q}(2,-1^{2}), or 𝒬⁡(22)\mathcal{Q}(2^{2}). If 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not hyperelliptic, the only 𝒬~\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}-periodic points are fixed points of the involution JJ. If 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is hyperelliptic, the only 𝒬~\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}-periodic points are fixed points for JJ and fixed points for the hyperelliptic involution.

In Section 4 we will recall the definition of rank, and in Corollary 4.3 we will see that 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), 𝒬⁡(2,−12)\mathcal{Q}(2,-1^{2}), and 𝒬⁡(22)\mathcal{Q}(2^{2}) are exactly the 𝒬\mathcal{Q} that have rank 1.

Theorem 1.4 is the most difficult of our main theorems, and we expect the combination of Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 to have the most applications.

Context. Lelièvre, Monteil, and Weiss recently showed that the only translation surfaces in which every pair of points are finitely blocked are covers of tori [LMW16]; we recover and strengthen this in Corollary 3.9. Generalizing work of Hubert, Schmoll, and Troubetzkoy [HST08] in the case of lattice surfaces, they also showed that for any point pp on any translation surface, the set of points not illuminated by pp is finite. For more background on the finite blocking problem and the closely related illumination problem, see [Mon05, Mon09, HST08, LMW16].

In the case of closed G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbits, Theorem 1.2 is due to Gutkin, Hubert, and Schmidt [GHS03] and was established independently by Möller using algebro-geometric methods [Möl06]. Möller also showed that for non-arithmetic closed orbits in genus 2 the only periodic points are Weierstrass points. Non-arithmetic closed orbits in genus 2 were classified by McMullen [McM05, McM06].

The proof of Theorem 1.3 builds upon and was inspired by an argument of Hubert, Schmoll, and Troubetzkoy [HST08, Theorem 5].

Lanneau classified connected components of strata of quadratic differentials [Lan08], see also [CM14] for a correction.

Apisa previously classified periodic points over connected components of strata of Abelian differentials: they exist only for hyperelliptic connected components, in which case they must be Weierstrass points [Api20]. We make use of one of the main technical lemmas of [Api20] in Section 6. As we point out in Remark 5.6, the strategy used to prove Theorem 1.4 does not work for strata of Abelian differentials, so our analysis does not recover Apisa’s result.

There is an unexpected periodic point over the golden eigenform locus in genus 2, see forthcoming work of Eskin-McMullen-Mukamel-Wright and [KM16].

Problem 1.5.

Compute the periodic points over the (Prym) eigenform loci and the Veech-Ward-Bouw-Möller Teichmüller curves, as well as the new orbit closures in the forthcoming work of Eskin-McMullen-Mukamel-Wright and [MMW17].

When studying translation surfaces without marked points it is often helpful to consider degenerations which may have marked points [MW17], and indeed Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 have already been used to study G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closures of unmarked translation surfaces [MW18].

Organization. Section 2 proves Theorem 1.3. Section 3 gives our applications to the finite blocking problem, including Theorem 1.1. The remaining sections, which are independent of Section 3, prove Theorem 1.4. Section 4 gives the required background, and Section 5 gives a proof, conditional on two results established in the remaining two sections. The approach is by induction: Section 6 produces an appropriate cylinder to degenerate, and Section 7 provides the base case.

2. Proof of Theorem 1.3

We begin with some preliminary observations.

Lemma 2.1.

Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be a point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M}, and let (X,ω,S)∈𝒩(X,\omega,S)\in\mathcal{N}. For each s∈Ss\in S, fix a path γs\gamma_{s} from a zero of ω\omega to ss. Then each branch of the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over (X,ω)(X,\omega) is locally defined by a collection of linear equations of the form

∑s∈Sas​∫γsω=∫γω,\sum_{s\in S}a_{s}\int_{\gamma_{s}}\omega=\int_{\gamma}\omega,

where as∈ℝa_{s}\in\mathbb{R}, and γ∈H1​(X,Σ,ℝ)\gamma\in H_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mathbb{R}), and Σ\Sigma is the set of zeros of ω\omega.

Moreover, these equations can be chosen to hold locally on 𝒩\mathcal{N}, and each fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over ℳ\mathcal{M} is either empty or has dimension dim𝒩−dimℳ\dim\mathcal{N}-\dim\mathcal{M}.

Note that ∫γω\int_{\gamma}\omega is locally constant on the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over (X,ω)(X,\omega), so in the first part of the statement we could have replaced it with a constant.

Proof.

Like all G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closures, 𝒩\mathcal{N} is locally defined by linear equations in local period coordinates. A basis for local period coordinates can be obtained from the γs\gamma_{s} together with a basis of H1​(X,Σ)H_{1}(X,\Sigma).

Since the equations hold locally on 𝒩\mathcal{N}, the dimension of 𝒩\mathcal{N} must be equal to the dimension of ℳ\mathcal{M} plus the dimension of a fiber; the dimension of the fiber is |S||S| minus the dimension of the span of the coefficient vectors (as)s∈S(a_{s})_{s\in S} arising from the linear equations locally defining the fiber. ∎

Note that the image of 𝒩\mathcal{N} in ℳ\mathcal{M} is G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) invariant and contains an open subset of ℳ\mathcal{M}, so by [EM18, EMM15] this image contains the complement of a union of smaller dimensional affine invariant sub-manifolds. However, as we now show, some fibers can indeed be empty.

Example 2.2.

Let ℳ⊂ℋ⁡(5,1)\mathcal{M}\subset\mathcal{H}(5,1) be the locus of double covers of surfaces in ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) that are branched over the zero and one other point pp. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the 2-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M} that marks the two pre-images of the image of pp under the hyperelliptic involution. Then the image of 𝒩\mathcal{N} in ℳ\mathcal{M} is the locus of covers where pp is not a Weierstrass point.

We now make one final preliminary remark before moving on to the main definition in this section. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be an irreducible 2-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M}, and let (X,ω,{p1,p2})∈𝒩(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\})\in\mathcal{N}.

If dim𝒩=dimℳ\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}, then 𝒩\mathcal{N} would be the fiberwise union of two periodic points, contradicting the fact that 𝒩\mathcal{N} is irreducible. On the other hand, if dim𝒩=dimℳ+2\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+2, then 𝒩\mathcal{N} would be the fiberwise union of two 1-point markings in which the single point is unconstrained, again contradicting the fact that 𝒩\mathcal{N} is irreducible. Hence, we get that dim𝒩=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1.

Let γi\gamma_{i} be a path from a zero of ω\omega to pip_{i}. By Lemma 2.1, the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over (X,ω)(X,\omega) is locally defined by a single equation of the form

a1​∫γ1ω+a2​∫γ1ω=∫γω,a_{1}\int_{\gamma_{1}}\omega+a_{2}\int_{\gamma_{1}}\omega=\int_{\gamma}\omega,

where γ∈H1​(X,Σ,ℝ)\gamma\in H_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mathbb{R}) and a1,a2∈ℝa_{1},a_{2}\in\mathbb{R}. If a1a_{1} was zero, then 𝒩\mathcal{N} would be the fiberwise union of 1-point marking containing (X,ω,{p1})(X,\omega,\{p_{1}\}), in which the single point is unconstrained, and a periodic point containing (X,ω,{p2})(X,\omega,\{p_{2}\}), yet again contradicting the fact that 𝒩\mathcal{N} is irreducible. So we conclude that both aia_{i} are non-zero.

Definition 2.3.

Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be an irreducible 2-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M}. As above, consider any (X,ω,{p1,p2})∈𝒩(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\})\in\mathcal{N}, and rewrite the linear equation locally defining the fiber in the form

∫γ1ω=a​∫γ2ω+∫γω,\int_{\gamma_{1}}\omega=a\int_{\gamma_{2}}\omega+\int_{\gamma}\omega,

with a≠0a\neq 0. We define the slope of 𝒩\mathcal{N} to be aa or 1/a1/a, whichever is larger in absolute value.

The slope describes the speed at which one marked point moves when the other marked point is moved at unit speed (and the underlying surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) without marked points is fixed). Note that if the role of p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} are interchanged, 1/a1/a will play the role of aa.

The slope depends only on 𝒩\mathcal{N} and not on any of the choices made in the definition. Indeed, over 𝒩\mathcal{N} there is a bundle whose fiber is first cohomology rel the singular points and the marked points. There is a rank two trivial subbundle spanned by the deformations that move the two marked points. (We are assuming the two marked points are labeled; if not, one can pass to a two-fold cover where they are labeled.) We can intersect T⁡(𝒩)T(\mathcal{N}) with this rank two trivial subbundle to get a trivial subbundle, and aa is the slope of that subbundle in each fiber.

Remark 2.4.

Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be an irreducible nn-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M} of dimension dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{M}+1. Then if (X,ω,S)∈𝒩(X,\omega,S)\in\mathcal{N} and p1,p2∈Sp_{1},p_{2}\in S, one can define the slope of p1p_{1} with respect to p2p_{2} in the same way. If (X,ω,S)(X,\omega,S) is generic, this will be equal to the slope of the irreducible 2-point marking given by the orbit closure of (X,ω,{p1,p2})(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\}).

Example 2.5.

If ℳ\mathcal{M} is the hyperelliptic locus in some stratum, and 𝒩\mathcal{N} is given by a pair of points that are exchanged under the hyperelliptic involution, then the slope is -1.

Example 2.6.

Suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} is an affine invariant submanifold of translation surfaces of genus gg, such that the generic translation surface in ℳ\mathcal{M} has a unique translation covering map to a translation surface of genus h<gh<g. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the set of all pairs of points on surfaces in ℳ\mathcal{M} that map to the same point on the associated surface of genus hh. Then 𝒩\mathcal{N} has slope 1.

Example 2.7.

Suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} is an arithmetic Teichmüller curve, so each surface (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M} admits a unique translation covering map ff of degree dd to a torus branched over one point. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be the locus of all pairs of points p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} on surfaces (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M} such that 2​f​(p1)=7​f​(p2)2f(p_{1})=7f(p_{2}), where we view the image torus as a group with origin equal to the image of the zeros of ω\omega. Then 𝒩\mathcal{N} has slope 7/27/2.

Theorem 2.8.

Suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} has only finitely many ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points. Then any irreducible 22-point marking 𝒩\mathcal{N} over ℳ\mathcal{M} has slope 11 or −1-1.

The proof is a generalization of [HST08, Proof of Theorem 5]. We will say that a point pp on a surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a periodic point if it is contained in a ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point, where ℳ\mathcal{M} is the orbit closure of (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Lemma 2.9.

Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be an irreducible 22-point marking over an affine invariant submanifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. Suppose that (X,ω)(X,\omega) has dense orbit in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Then if (X,ω,{p1,p2})∈𝒩(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\})\in\mathcal{N} and p1p_{1} is ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic, then p2p_{2} is also ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic.

Furthermore, if (X,ω,{p1,p2})(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\}) is in the closure of the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over (X,ω)(X,\omega) and p1p_{1} is a zero of ω\omega, then p2p_{2} is either a zero of ω\omega or an ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point.

Similarly, if (X,ω,{p1,p2})(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\}) is in the closure of the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over (X,ω)(X,\omega) and p1=p2p_{1}=p_{2}, then p1p_{1} is a ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point or a zero.

As in Remark 2.4, Lemma 2.9 can also be applied to irreducible nn-point markings 𝒩\mathcal{N} with dim𝒩=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1, by forgetting all but two points.

Proof.

Let 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} be the orbit closure of (X,ω,{p1,p2})(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\}), where p1p_{1} is ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic. This affine invariant submanifold must be properly contained in 𝒩\mathcal{N}, because at the generic point of 𝒩\mathcal{N} neither of the marked points are periodic.

By the discussion before Definition 2.3, dim𝒩=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1. Since 𝒩′⊊𝒩\mathcal{N}^{\prime}\subsetneq\mathcal{N}, we must have dim𝒩′=dimℳ\dim\mathcal{N}^{\prime}=\dim\mathcal{M}, and hence both p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} are ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic.

Now, suppose to a contradiction that p1p_{1} is a zero of ω\omega and p2p_{2} is neither a zero nor an ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point. Then the G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω,p1,p2)(X,\omega,p_{1},p_{2}) has dimension dimℳ+1=dim𝒩\dim\mathcal{M}+1=\dim\mathcal{N} and contains the set of (X,ω,p1,p2′)(X,\omega,p_{1},p_{2}^{\prime}) where p2′p_{2}^{\prime} is arbitrary.

We can now use either general principles or concrete arguments. The general principle is that the orbit closure of (X,ω,p1,p2)(X,\omega,p_{1},p_{2}) is contained in the boundary of 𝒩\mathcal{N} (in the Hodge bundle over ℳg,2\mathcal{M}_{g,2}), and by [MW17] or [Fil16b] this boundary must have dimension strictly smaller than dim𝒩\dim\mathcal{N}. One concrete argument, which we only sketch, is that the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over (X,ω)(X,\omega) consists of linear submanifolds of (X,ω)×(X,ω)(X,\omega)\times(X,\omega) of slope aa, and such submanifolds cannot accumulate on the set of (X,ω,p1,p2′)(X,\omega,p_{1},p_{2}^{\prime}), which has infinite slope.

The proof of the final claim is almost identical. ∎

Proof of Theorem 2.8.

Suppose otherwise. Consider (X,ω,{p1,p2})∈𝒩(X,\omega,\{p_{1},p_{2}\})\in\mathcal{N} such that the G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit of (X,ω)(X,\omega) is dense in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Let Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} be the finite set of all zeros of ω\omega together with all points of (X,ω)(X,\omega) contained in ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points. By assumption Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} is finite.

We consider the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} over (X,ω)(X,\omega); by the discussion in Definition 2.3, it must be one dimensional. Any path that pushes the point p1p_{1} around (X,ω)(X,\omega) while avoiding the set Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} can be lifted to a path in the fiber that pushes p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} around (X,ω)(X,\omega). By Lemma 2.9, along any such path where p1p_{1} avoids Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, the point p2p_{2} does not collide with either p1p_{1} or Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}.

As we move p1p_{1} on (X,ω)(X,\omega), p2p_{2} moves in a way determined by the slope so that the marked surface remains in the fiber. After possibly swapping the role of p1p_{1} and p2p_{2}, we may assume that when p1p_{1} moves with unit speed the point p2p_{2} moves with speed strictly less than unit speed.

By Lemma 2.9, when p1p_{1} is moved to a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, it must be the case that p2p_{2} is also moved to a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. Let α\alpha be a saddle connection on (X,ω,Σ′)(X,\omega,\Sigma^{\prime}) (that is, a straight line segment from a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} to a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} whose interior is disjoint from Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}) of minimal length. Move p1p_{1} to be on α\alpha, and then move p1p_{1} from one end of α\alpha to the other. At either end, p1p_{1} is at a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, so p2p_{2} must also be at a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. This is a contradiction because p1p_{1} moves strictly faster than p2p_{2} and because α\alpha is a minimal length saddle connection. ∎

Lemma 2.10.

Suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} has only finitely many ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be an irreducible nn-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M} with dim𝒩=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1. For every (X,ω,S)∈𝒩(X,\omega,S)\in\mathcal{N} there is a translation covering map ff to a half-translation surface such that ff maps SS to a point.

If the slope of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is 1, then ff can be chosen to map to a translation (rather than half-translation) surface.

Proof.

We first prove the main claim.

It suffices to prove the lemma when (X,ω,S)(X,\omega,S) has dense orbit in 𝒩\mathcal{N}, so we assume this. The reason it is sufficient is because if the conclusion holds on a dense subset of 𝒩\mathcal{N}, then it holds on all of 𝒩\mathcal{N}, and a dense subset of 𝒩\mathcal{N} has dense orbit.

Suppose, for some n′>nn^{\prime}>n, that there is an irreducible n′n^{\prime}-point marking 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} over ℳ\mathcal{M} of dimension dim𝒩=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1, such that for all (Y,η,P′)(Y,\eta,P^{\prime}) in 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} minus a union of smaller affine invariant submanifolds there is a set P⊂P′P\subset P^{\prime} so that (Y,η,P)∈𝒩(Y,\eta,P)\in\mathcal{N}.

In other words, in 𝒩\mathcal{N} there are nn marked points whose position locally determine each other given the unmarked translation surface, and 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} extends these nn points to a larger collection of points such that each locally determines all the others.

Let Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} be the set of zeros of ω\omega and all points ss such that (X,ω,s)(X,\omega,s) is contained in an ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point.

Sublemma 2.11.

Let TT be the sum of the cone angles at points of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, divided by π\pi. Then n′≤Tn^{\prime}\leq T.

Proof.

Consider (X,ω,S′)∈𝒩′(X,\omega,S^{\prime})\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime}, and move the n′n^{\prime}-marked points around while remaining in the fiber of 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} over (X,ω)(X,\omega). Move one of the marked points along a horizontal separatrix until it hits a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. By Lemma 2.9, all marked points must then lie at points of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}.

By Theorem 2.8, the slope for any pair of these points is 11 or −1-1, so each marked point must have traveled along a different directed horizontal line segment towards a point of Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. There are exactly TT such directed horizontal line segments. The claim is proved. ∎

Now assume n′n^{\prime} as above was maximal, which is possible by Sublemma 2.11. Let 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} be a corresponding n′n^{\prime}-point marking.

Sublemma 2.12.

Suppose that pp and qq are two points in (X,ω)−Σ′(X,\omega)-\Sigma^{\prime}, possibly equal. Say that p∼qp\sim q if there is a collection SS of n′n^{\prime} points containing pp and qq and such that (X,ω,S)∈𝒩′(X,\omega;S)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime}. Then ∼\sim is an equivalence relation on (X,ω)−Σ′(X,\omega)-\Sigma^{\prime}.

Proof of Sublemma 2.12:

Recall that Lemma 2.9 gives that if (X,ω,S)∈𝒩′(X,\omega;S)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime} and one point of SS is in Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}, then all points of SS are in Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}.

We begin with a subtle point, which is that p∼pp\sim p for all p∈(X,ω)−Σ′p\in(X,\omega)-\Sigma^{\prime}, for which we need to prove that for all pp, we can find SS containing pp so that (X,ω,S)∈𝒩′(X,\omega;S)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime}. As discussed previously, in the fiber over (X,ω)(X,\omega), the position of one of the n′n^{\prime} points locally determines the position of the other n′−1n^{\prime}-1 points. Lemma 2.9 implies that as we move one point in (X,ω)∖Σ′(X,\omega)\setminus\Sigma^{\prime}, the other points stay in (X,ω)∖Σ′(X,\omega)\setminus\Sigma^{\prime} and that none of the n′n^{\prime} points collide with each other. So, we can see that p∼pp\sim p by starting with any (X,ω,S)∈𝒩′(X,\omega;S)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime}, and moving SS so that it contains pp.

If ∼\sim is not an equivalence relation, then there are two sets of n′n^{\prime}-points, both in 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime}, that partially overlap. Let S′′S^{\prime\prime} denote their union, and let 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} denote the orbit closure of (X,ω,S′′)(X,\omega,S^{\prime\prime}). Since we have assumed (X,ω)(X,\omega) has dense orbit, 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} is a point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M}.

We now show that dim𝒩′′=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1 and that 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} is irreducible. Indeed, 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} is a component of

{(X,ω,S∪S′):(X,ω,S)∈𝒩′,(X,ω,S′)∈𝒩′,|S∪S′|=|S′′|}.\{(X,\omega,S\cup S^{\prime}):(X,\omega,S)\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime},(X,\omega,S^{\prime})\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime},|S\cup S^{\prime}|=|S^{\prime\prime}|\}.

In fibers of 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime}, the position of each point locally determines the position of all the others. Since S∩S′≠∅S\cap S^{\prime}\neq\emptyset, we get the same statement for fibers of 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime}, proving dim𝒩′′=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1 and that 𝒩′′\mathcal{N}^{\prime\prime} is irreducible. This contradicts the maximality of n′n^{\prime}. ∎

Let Q0Q_{0} denote the quotient of (X,ω)∖Σ′(X,\omega)\setminus\Sigma^{\prime} by the equivalence relation ∼\sim. We claim that the map (X,ω)∖Σ′→Q0(X,\omega)\setminus\Sigma^{\prime}\to Q_{0} is a covering map. Indeed, suppose that (X,ω,{z1,⋯,zn′})∈𝒩′(X,\omega,\{z_{1},\cdots,z_{n^{\prime}}\})\in\mathcal{N}^{\prime}, and that none of the ziz_{i} are in Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. For some ε>0\varepsilon>0, the ε\varepsilon balls about the ziz_{i} are embedded, disjoint, and disjoint from Σ′\Sigma^{\prime}. Since each marked point moves at speed 11 or −1-1 with respect to each other marked point, each point in the ball Bε​(zi)B_{\varepsilon}(z_{i}) is equivalent to a point in Bε​(zj)B_{\varepsilon}(z_{j}) for each j≠ij\neq i. The quotient by the equivalence relation identified all these balls to a single ball. This shows that the map is a covering map, and hence that the quotient is a surface.

Furthermore, the composition of the map from Bε​(zi)B_{\varepsilon}(z_{i}) to Q0Q_{0} with the inverse of the map from Bε​(zj)B_{\varepsilon}(z_{j}) to Q0Q_{0} is given in local coordinates by multiplication by 11 or −1-1. Hence the quotient has an atlas of charts to ℂ\mathbb{C} whose transition functions are translations and translations composed with multiplication by −1-1. The quotient map is a local isometry, so the quotient is a punctured surface.

The quotient map extends continuously to a map ff from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to the metric completion of the punctured surface Q0Q_{0}, and this ff is the desired map.

If the slope of 𝒩\mathcal{N} is 1, a slight variant of the above gives the final claim, modifying the proof by picking 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} to be a maximal point marking containing 𝒩\mathcal{N} subject to the condition that any pair of points in 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} has slope 1. ∎

Lemma 2.13.

Suppose that ℳ\mathcal{M} has only finitely many ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points. Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be an irreducible nn-point marking with n>2n>2. Then dim𝒩=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1.

Proof.

Suppose the lemma is not true. Consider a counterexample with nn as small as possible.

Pick (X,ω,S)∈𝒩(X,\omega,S)\in\mathcal{N} such that the G​L+​(2,ℝ)GL^{+}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit of (X,ω,S)(X,\omega,S) is dense in 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Because of the minimality of nn, no point of SS locally determines the position of any of the others. Hence the same remains true if we forget a point pp in SS; so no irreducible piece 𝒩′\mathcal{N}^{\prime} of the orbit closure of (X,ω,S−{p})(X,\omega,S-\{p\}) satisfies dim𝒩′=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}^{\prime}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1, unless it is given by a single unconstrained marked point. Hence, again because of the minimality assumption, the orbit closure of (X,ω,S−{p})(X,\omega,S-\{p\}) is given by n−1n-1 unconstrained points. We conclude that the fiber of (X,ω)(X,\omega) is locally defined by a single equation on the points of SS. By irreducibly this equation must involve all the points.

If, for each p∈Sp\in S, we let γp\gamma_{p} be a path from a zero of ω\omega to pp, this equation can be written as

∑ai​∫γpiω=∫γω\sum a_{i}\int_{\gamma_{p_{i}}}\omega=\int_{\gamma}\omega

for some γ∈H1​(X,Σ,ℝ)\gamma\in H^{1}(X,\Sigma,\mathbb{R}) and some non-zero real numbers aia_{i}.

We will use the following to finish the proof.

Sublemma 2.14.

If |S|>3|S|>3, or if |S|=3|S|=3 and a2+a3≠0a_{2}+a_{3}\neq 0, then it is possible to move in the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} so that p1p_{1} collides with a zero, but the other points of SS do not collide with each other or with zeros.

If |S|=3|S|=3 and a1+a2≠0a_{1}+a_{2}\neq 0 and a1+a2+a3≠0a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}\neq 0, then it is possible to move in the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} so that p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} collide, but that p3p_{3} does not collide with p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} or a zero.

It seems likely that Sublemma 2.14 could be justified or avoided in different ways; we give one justification now. Note that, if, for example, a2+a3=0a_{2}+a_{3}=0, then p2p_{2} and p3p_{3} might collide and become a single unconstrained point.

Proof.

We first prove the first statement. For convenience, rotate the surface to assume without loss of generality that p1p_{1} lies on a vertical line segment starting at a point of Σ\Sigma (also known as a separatrix). As we now show, we can then make a perturbation so that p1p_{1} is the only point of SS that lies on vertical line segment starting at a point of Σ\Sigma, while remaining in the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Indeed, in local coordinates, this deformation needs to move each pi,i>1p_{i},i>1 off of a countable collection of vertical lines. (These arise from finitely many vertical separatrices, which wind around the surface and may intersect a small piece of the surface countably many times.) Because we know the fiber is locally defined by one linear equation as above, we can see that, even while fixing the position of p1p_{1}, each pip_{i} can be moved off any vertical line segment. So in fact almost every deformation of SS fixing p1p_{1} and staying in the fiber of 𝒩\mathcal{N} will work.

We now claim that it is possible to choose the deformation so that moreover afterwards no two points of SS are joined by a vertical line segment. If this is not possible, there must be two points, say p2p_{2} and p3p_{3}, so that p3p_{3} remains on the vertical line through p2p_{2} in all deformations fixing p1p_{1}. This is only possible if n=3n=3 and a3=−a2a_{3}=-a_{2}.

Now, we can move SS while keeping constant the real parts of the periods of all the γi\gamma_{i}, so that p1p_{1} moves along a vertical line segment to a point of Σ\Sigma. Since each point of SS travels along a vertical line, this does not cause any of the other points of SS to collide with each other or with Σ\Sigma. This proves the first statement.

We now prove the second statement. Perturbing the marked points, we can assume there is a line segment between p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} not parallel to any other line segment joining points of Σ∪{p1,p2}\Sigma\cup\{p_{1},p_{2}\}; without loss of generality this segment is vertical.

First suppose that, no matter how we do this, p3p_{3} lies on a vertical line segment starting at a point of Σ\Sigma. Then, as we move p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} equally to the right, p3p_{3} must be unchanged, so we conclude that a1+a2=0a_{1}+a_{2}=0, a contradiction.

Next suppose that, no matter how we do this, that p3p_{3} lies on the continuation of the vertical line segment containing p1p_{1} and p2p_{2}. Similarly this contradicts our assumption that a1+a2+a3≠0a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}\neq 0.

So we can assume that p3p_{3} does not lie on the continuation of the vertical line segment joining p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} or on a vertical line segment starting at a point of Σ\Sigma. Now we can use a deformation that fixes real periods to collide p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} without colliding p3p_{3} with p1,p2p_{1},p_{2} or Σ\Sigma. ∎

If |S|>3|S|>3, use Sublemma 2.14 to move one of the points of SS to a point of Σ\Sigma. This gives a new point marking that, by [MW17], is defined by a single equation and contradicts the minimality of nn. Hence n=3n=3.

Now that we know n=3n=3, first suppose that |a2|≠|a3||a_{2}|\neq|a_{3}|. Use Sublemma 2.14 to move p1p_{1} into a point of Σ\Sigma. We can assume that γp1\gamma_{p_{1}} was a path from the zero that p1p_{1} collides with to p1p_{1}, so that γp1\gamma_{p_{1}} becomes a constant path after this collision. We get a two-point marking defined by

a2​∫γp2ω+a3​∫γp3ω=∫γω.a_{2}\int_{\gamma_{p_{2}}}\omega+a_{3}\int_{\gamma_{p_{3}}}\omega=\int_{\gamma}\omega.

This contradicts Theorem 2.8, because it is an irreducible 2-point marking of slope not equal to ±1\pm 1.

Next suppose that |a1|=|a2|=|a3||a_{1}|=|a_{2}|=|a_{3}|. We can assume that a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} have the same sign, so a1+a2≠0a_{1}+a_{2}\neq 0 and |a1+a2|≠|a3||a_{1}+a_{2}|\neq|a_{3}|. Use Sublemma 2.14 to collide p1p_{1} and p2p_{2}. This gives a two-point marking defined by

(a1+a2)​∫γp1ω+a3​∫γp3ω=∫γ+a2​(γp1−γp2)ω,(a_{1}+a_{2})\int_{\gamma_{p_{1}}}\omega+a_{3}\int_{\gamma_{p_{3}}}\omega=\int_{\gamma+a_{2}(\gamma_{p_{1}}-\gamma_{p_{2}})}\omega,

where we note that since p1=p2p_{1}=p_{2}, the path γp1−γp2\gamma_{p_{1}}-\gamma_{p_{2}} gives a class in H1​(X,Σ,ℝ)H_{1}(X,\Sigma,\mathbb{R}). Again this contradicts Theorem 2.8. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

By Theorem 1.2, there are only finitely many ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points. By Lemma 2.13, we have dim𝒩=dimℳ+1\dim\mathcal{N}=\dim\mathcal{M}+1. Hence Lemma 2.10 gives the result. ∎

Remark 2.15.

Note that while this section has considered only translation surfaces, the results in this section hold almost verbatim for half-translation surfaces as well, except that for half-translation surfaces the slope of a point marking is only well-defined up to sign.

3. The finite blocking problem

In the first subsection we explain the implications of Theorem 1.3 for finitely blocked points; in the next two we give applications; and in the final subsection we study possible finite blocking sets. The final three subsections can be read independently of each other but all rely on the first.

3.1. Consequences of Theorem 1.3

Throughout this subsection let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface. Given two not necessarily distinct points x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} on (X,ω)(X,\omega) the finite blocking problem asks whether all straight line paths between x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} may be blocked by a finite collection of points BB. If this is possible then we say that x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are blocked by BB. The following lemma provides an example of this phenomenon.

Lemma 3.1.

Suppose that (X,ω)(X,\omega) has an involution jj so that j∗​ω=−ωj^{*}\omega=-\omega. For any point pp that is not a zero and is not fixed by jj, pp and j⁡(p)j(p) are finitely blocked by the fixed points of jj.

Proof.

Let ℓ\ell be a line segment in (X,ω)(X,\omega) joining pp to j⁡(p)j(p). Since j∗​ω=−ωj^{*}\omega=-\omega, we get that jj maps ℓ\ell to itself, and hence contains a fixed point in its interior. ∎

Lelièvre, Monteil, and Weiss showed that if (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a translation cover of a torus then any two points are finitely blocked (and, conversely, that this property characterizes torus covers) [LMW16, Theorem 1]. Hence, in the remainder of this section, we make the following standing assumption.

Assumption 3.2.

Suppose throughout this section that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not a translation cover of a torus.

Recall the result of Möller that states that, with this assumption, there is a unique translation covering map πXmin:(X,ω)→(Xmin,ωmin)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}:(X,\omega)\to(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}) to a translation surface of minimal genus, and any map from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to a translation surface is a factor of this map [Möl06, Theorem 2.6]. This can be extended to quadratic differentials as follows.

Lemma 3.3.

There is a quadratic differential (Qmin,qmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}) with a degree 1 or 2 translation covering map (Xmin,ωmin)→(Qmin,qmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}})\to(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}) such that any translation covering map from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to a quadratic differential is a factor of the composite map πQmin:(X,ω)→(Qmin,qmin)\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}:(X,\omega)\to(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}).

Remark 3.4.

Before giving the proof, we recall a consequence of Möller’s result. Suppose that XX has an automorphism TT with T∗​ω=ξ−1​ωT^{*}\omega=\xi^{-1}\omega, where ξ\xi is a primitive kk-th root of unity. Then

ξ−1∘π∘T:(X,ω)→(Xmin,ξmin−1​ωmin)\xi^{-1}\circ\pi\circ T:(X,\omega)\to(X_{\operatorname{min}},\xi_{\operatorname{min}}^{-1}\omega_{\operatorname{min}})

is another translation covering from (X,ω)(X,\omega) to a surface of the same genus, where in the definition of the covering ξ−1\xi^{-1} denotes a rotation map (Xmin,ωmin)→(Xmin,ξmin−1​ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}})\to(X_{\operatorname{min}},\xi_{\operatorname{min}}^{-1}\omega_{\operatorname{min}}). The uniqueness of this map implies there is a map t:Xmin→Xmint:X_{\operatorname{min}}\to X_{\operatorname{min}} satisfying t∗​ωmin=ξ−1​ωmint^{*}\omega_{\operatorname{min}}=\xi^{-1}\omega_{\operatorname{min}} and π∘T=t∘π\pi\circ T=t\circ\pi. This tt might have smaller order than that of TT, but of course the order of tt is a multiple of kk.

Proof.

If (X,ω)(X,\omega) does not admit any translation covering maps to strictly half translation surfaces, we may set (Qmin,qmin)=(Xmin,ωmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}})=(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}).

So suppose there is a translation covering map h:(X,ω)→(Q′,q′)h:(X,\omega)\to(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}), where (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) is not the square of an Abelian differential. Recall that any translation covering map from a translation surface to a quadratic differential lifts to a map from the translation surface to the square root of the quadratic differential. Let (X′,ω′)→(Q′,q′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})\to(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) be the square root of (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}), and let JJ be the involution on (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) so (Q′,q′)=(X′,ω′)/J(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime})=(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})/J. By the defining property of (Xmin,ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}), there exists a translation covering map π:(X′,ω′)→(Xmin,ωmin)\pi:(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})\to(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}), and by the previous remark we get an automorphism jj negating ωmin\omega_{\operatorname{min}} and satisfying π=j∘π∘J\pi=j\circ\pi\circ J.

Since (Xmin,ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}) does not cover a smaller genus translation surface, we get that jj must be an involution, and also that (Xmin,ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}) has at most one involution negating ωmin\omega_{\operatorname{min}}. Hence the lemma is true with (Qmin,qmin)=(Xmin,ωmin)/j(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}})=(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}})/j. ∎

We define a point in a point marking to be free if it can be moved freely, independently of the unmarked surface and the position of the other points in the point marking.

Remark 3.5.

We now clarify the structure of irreducible point markings, justifying our previous remark that they arise from covering constructions.

Given ℳ\mathcal{M}, let ℳmin\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{min}} denote the set of all (Qmin,qmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}) arising from all (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M}. There is a natural point marking ℳminbr\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{min}}^{\mathrm{br}} over ℳmin\mathcal{M}_{\operatorname{min}} which consists of all (Qmin,qmin,B)(Q_{\mathrm{min}},q_{\mathrm{min}},B) such that there is a cover (X,ω)→(Qmin,qmin)(X,\omega)\to(Q_{\mathrm{min}},q_{\mathrm{min}}) branched over BB, with (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M} and BB of maximal size. If 𝒩\mathcal{N} is an irreducible nn-point marking over ℳ\mathcal{M} with n>1n>1, then for each (X,ω,S)∈𝒩(X,\omega,S)\in\mathcal{N}, Theorem 1.3 gives that SS maps to a single point p∈(Qmin,qmin)p\in(Q_{\mathrm{min}},q_{\mathrm{min}}). We can then consider the point marking 𝒩min\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{min}} which consists of all (Qmin,qmin,B∪{p})(Q_{\mathrm{min}},q_{\mathrm{min}},B\cup\{p\}) that arise in this way. By Theorem 1.3, the point marking 𝒩min\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{min}} over ℳmin\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{min}} consists of a number of 𝒩min\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{min}}-periodic points together with a number of free marked points.

Note that in general SS could be a proper subset of the fiber of pp; we have qmin​(S)={p}q_{\mathrm{min}}(S)=\{p\} but not always S=qmin−1​(qmin​(S))S=q_{\mathrm{min}}^{-1}(q_{\mathrm{min}}(S)). We also have that pp must be free; it cannot be an 𝒩min\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{min}}-periodic point.

Theorem 3.6.

If x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are finitely blocked on (X,ω)(X,\omega), then either they are both ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points or zeros, where ℳ\mathcal{M} is the orbit closure of (X,ω)(X,\omega), or πQmin​(x1)=πQmin​(x2)\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1})=\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{2}).

To prove this theorem, which is the main result of this subsection, we first require two lemmas. Given two points x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} that are finitely blocked by a collection of points BB, let ℳx1,x2,B\mathcal{M}_{x_{1},x_{2},B} be the GL2​(ℝ)\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω,p,q,B)(X,\omega;p,q;B) in ℋ∗n+2\mathcal{H}^{*n+2} where nn is the size of BB. We permit the points x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} to coincide and to be zeros, in which case we use the same notation, but take the orbit closure in ℋ∗n+1\mathcal{H}^{*n+1} or ℋ∗n\mathcal{H}^{*n}. Finally, in order to refer to specific zeros, we will work on a finite cover of ℳ\mathcal{M} where the zeros are labeled. We will suppress these details in the sequel.

Lemma 3.7.

If (X′,ω′,x1′,x2′,B′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime};x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime};B^{\prime}) belongs to ℳx1,x2,B\mathcal{M}_{x_{1},x_{2},B} then x1′x_{1}^{\prime} and x2′x_{2}^{\prime} are blocked by B′B^{\prime}.

Proof.

The locus of (X′,ω′,x1′,x2′,B′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime};x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime};B^{\prime}) such that there is a straight line segment from x1′x_{1}^{\prime} to x2′x_{2}^{\prime} not intersecting B′B^{\prime} or the zeros of ω′\omega^{\prime} is open and GL2​(ℝ)\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) invariant. Therefore, its complement is closed and GL2​(ℝ)\mathrm{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})-invariant and hence contains ℳx1,x2,B\mathcal{M}_{x_{1},x_{2},B} since it contains (X,ω,x1,x2,B)(X,\omega;x_{1},x_{2},B). ∎

We define a blocking set to be minimal if no proper subset also blocks the two points.

Lemma 3.8.

Neither x1x_{1} nor x2x_{2} is free in ℳx1,x2,B\mathcal{M}_{x_{1},x_{2},B}. If BB is minimal, then locally in ℳx1,x2,B\mathcal{M}_{x_{1},x_{2},B} the position of the points in BB are determined by the unmarked surface and x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}.

Moreover, either

  1. (1)

    ℳx1,x2,B\mathcal{M}_{x_{1},x_{2},B} consists entirely of periodic points, or

  2. (2)

    ℳx1,x2,B\mathcal{M}_{x_{1},x_{2},B} consists of periodic points and one other irreducible piece which contains at least one of x1x_{1} or x2x_{2}.

Proof.

If x1x_{1} is free, we can move it into a small ball around x2x_{2} that doesn’t contain any points of BB, and find a straight line segment from x1x_{1} to x2x_{2} not intersecting BB.

If some points in BB could be moved without changing the underlying unmarked surface or the position of x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}, we could move at least one of these points off the countable collection of line segments from x1x_{1} to x2x_{2} to obtain a smaller finite blocking set. This proves the first statement.

Given the first statement, if the second statement did not hold, then x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} would have to be contained in different irreducible pieces that are not periodic points, and there could be no other irreducible pieces that are not periodic points. Pick a surface in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and move x1x_{1} so it is not a periodic point. Then move x2x_{2} to x1x_{1}. If x2x_{2} collided with another point of its irreducible piece as it arrives at x1x_{1}, this would prove that x1x_{1} is in fact a periodic point, by Lemma 2.9. Hence x2x_{2} can be moved very close to x1x_{1} without another point of its irreducible piece moving close to x1x_{1}. This is a contradiction, because we can then find a straight line segment from x1x_{1} to x2x_{2} not intersecting BB. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.6.

Let BB be a minimal finite blocking set.

First we suppose that x1x_{1} is ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic or a zero and show that so is x2x_{2}. Indeed, move x2x_{2} very close to x1x_{1}. Since all points in the point marking are either fixed or move with slope ±1\pm 1 with respect to x2x_{2}, there cannot always be a point of BB in between x2x_{2} and x1x_{1}. This gives a contradiction to the assumption that x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are blocked by BB.

Next suppose neither x1x_{1} nor x2x_{2} is periodic. By the previous lemma and Theorem 1.3 they must map to the same point under πQmin\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}. ∎

Corollary 3.9.

A non-singular point on a translation surface that is not a torus-cover is only finitely blocked from finitely many other points.

Proof.

Let pp be a non-singular point on a translation surface that is not a torus cover. If pp is periodic then it is only finitely blocked from other periodic points, of which there are finitely many by Theorem 1.2. If pp is not periodic then it is only finitely blocked from other points in πQmin−1​(πQmin​(p))\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}^{-1}\left(\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(p)\right), of which there are only finitely many. ∎

3.2. kk-differentials, k>2k>2.

Throughout this section we will suppose that (S,θ)(S,\theta) is a Riemann surface SS with a meromorphic finite area kk-differential θ\theta, k>2k>2, and θ\theta is not a power of a lower order differential. Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be the canonical unfolding of (S,θ)(S,\theta) to an Abelian differential, which comes with a map πS:(X,ω)→(S,θ)\pi_{S}:(X,\omega)\to(S,\theta). In this section we will prove the following:

Theorem 3.10.

If (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not a translation covering of a torus then there are only finitely many pairs of finitely blocked points on (S,θ)(S,\theta).

Proof.

XX has a rotational self-symmetry TT of order kk with (S,θ)=(X,ω)/⟨T⟩(S,\theta)=(X,\omega)/\langle T\rangle. By Remark 3.4, we see that it descends to an automorphism tt of XminX_{\operatorname{min}}, with πXmin∘T=t∘πXmin\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}\circ T=t\circ\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}.

If s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} are finitely blocked on (S,θ)(S,\theta), then the set πS−1​(s1)\pi_{S}^{-1}(s_{1}) is finitely blocked from the set π−1​(s2)\pi^{-1}(s_{2}), which means there is a finite set BB such that every straight line segment from one set to the other intersects BB. Equivalently, every point of one set is finitely blocked from every point in the second set.

Suppose that s1s_{1} or s2s_{2} is such that πS−1​(s1)\pi_{S}^{-1}(s_{1}) and πS−1​(s2)\pi_{S}^{-1}(s_{2}) do not contain any ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic points and do not map to any of the finitely many points in (Xmin,ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}) that are fixed by a non-trivial power of tt. (As usual, ℳ\mathcal{M} is the orbit closure of (X,ω)(X,\omega).)

We will show that s1s_{1} and s2s_{2} are not finitely blocked. Suppose in order to find a contradiction that they are. Consider a point of πS−1​(s1)\pi_{S}^{-1}(s_{1}) and a point of πS−1​(s2)\pi_{S}^{-1}(s_{2}). Since these two points are finitely blocked, Theorem 3.6 gives that they map to the same point in (Qmin,qmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}). Hence πQmin\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}} maps πS−1​(s1)\pi_{S}^{-1}(s_{1}) to a single point of (Qmin,qmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}). But πS−1​(s1)\pi_{S}^{-1}(s_{1}) is a TT orbit, so its image on (Xmin,ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}) must be a tt orbit of size at most two, which is a contradiction since k>2k>2. ∎

Recall that our convention is that polygons are assumed to have connected boundary.

Proposition 3.11.

A rational polygon unfolds to the cover of a torus if and only if the polygon is Gaussian, Eisenstein, or rectangle-tiled.

Proof.

Let PP be a rational polygon and suppose its unfolding (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a torus cover; we will show PP is Gaussian, Eisenstein, or rectangle-tiled. (The other direction is easy.)

Let kk be the least common denominator of the angles divided by π\pi, so XX admits an order kk symmetry TT with T∗​(ω)=ξ​ωT^{*}(\omega)=\xi\omega, where ξ\xi is a primitive kk-th root of unity. The symmetry TT arises in the definition of the unfolding of PP, and the quotient of XX by ⟨T⟩\langle T\rangle can be understood as two copies of the PP glued together to form a sphere, often called the pillowcase double of PP.

By assumption, ω\omega lies in a two dimensional subspace of H1​(X,ℂ)H^{1}(X,\mathbb{C}) defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, spanned by ω\omega and its complex conjugate. Since T∗​(ω)=ξ​ωT^{*}(\omega)=\xi\omega, this subspace is invariant under T∗T^{*}. Hence T∗T^{*} restricted to this rational subspace must have all Galois conjugates of ξ\xi as eigenvalues. Hence, the degree of ℚ⁡(ξ)\mathbb{Q}(\xi) as a field extension of ℚ\mathbb{Q} is at most 2, and we conclude that k∈{2,3,4,6}k\in\{2,3,4,6\}.

For each zero of ω\omega there is some non-trivial power of TT that fixes it. Indeed, a zero of ω\omega that was not fixed by any non-trivial power of PP would give rise to a cone angle of the pillowcase double of angle at least 4​π4\pi, which is a contradiction because we have assumed that PP does not have any slits. Hence if p:H1​(X,Σ,ℂ)→H1​(X,ℂ)p:H^{1}(X,\Sigma,\mathbb{C})\to H^{1}(X,\mathbb{C}) is the usual map from cohomology relative to the set Σ\Sigma of zeros of ω\omega to absolute cohomology, we get that TT acting on ker⁡(p)\ker(p) does not have any primitive kk-th roots of unity as eigenvalues. (Here we count preimages of corners of PP of angle πk\frac{\pi}{k} as zeros of order zero and include them in Σ\Sigma.) Indeed, ker⁡(p)\ker(p), viewed as a representation of ℤ/n\mathbb{Z}/n via the action of TT, is a sub-representation of a direct sum of representations of ℤ/n\mathbb{Z}/n that factor through smaller groups. Hence the dimension of the ξ\xi-eigenspace of TT is the same in absolute and relative cohomology.

The sum of primitive eigenspaces of TT in relative and absolute cohomology are both defined over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Since pp induces a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear isomorphism between them it follows that the relative periods of ω\omega are rational linear combinations of the absolute periods of ω\omega.

If k∈{3,4,6}k\in\{3,4,6\} then the periods span a lattice in ℂ\mathbb{C}, and after rotating and scaling the relative periods lie in ℚ⁡[ξ]\mathbb{Q}[\xi]. Since the sides of PP are all periods, we can, up to rescaling, assume that the vertices of PP lie in ℤ⁡[ξ]\mathbb{Z}[\xi]. We can also assume that some edge of PP is horizontal, by rotating and scaling. Since all angles of PP are multiples of π/k\pi/k, we get that all edges have angle a multiple of π/k\pi/k with horizontal.

First suppose k=4k=4. Then the vertices of PP are in ℤ⁡[i]\mathbb{Z}[i]. Starting with the usual 1 by 1 square grid, we can subdivide each square into 8 triangles so that the center of the square and the center of each edge, as well as the four corners of the square, are the vertices. Then it is easy to see that all edges of PP are unions of edges of this triangulation of the plane, and hence that PP is Gaussian.

Next suppose k∈{3,6}k\in\{3,6\}. Then the vertices of PP are vertices in the usual tiling of the plane by equilateral triangles. We can similarly subdivide each equilateral triangle into six triangles, and again get that all the edges of PP are unions of edges of this triangulation of the plane, and hence that PP is Eisenstein.

If k=2k=2 then after rotating and scaling the relative periods lie in ℤ⁡[i​a]\mathbb{Z}[ia] for some real number aa and the polygon is rectangle-tiled. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

If PP is Gaussian or Eisenstein, then it unfolds to a torus cover, where it is known that any two points are finitely blocked. Hence any two sets of points are finitely blocked (just take the union of the blocking sets).

Suppose now that PP is not Gaussian or Eisenstein. By Proposition 3.11, PP does not unfold to a torus cover and so there are only finitely many periodic points on the unfolding and any point is finitely blocked from only finitely many others by Theorem 3.6. If some angle is not an integer multiple of π2\frac{\pi}{2} then the pillowcase double of PP is a kk-differential for k>2k>2 and so Theorem 3.10 implies that there are only finitely many pairs of finitely blocked points on PP. ∎

3.3. Prime triangles.

Theorem 1.3 can sometimes be applied without knowing the orbit closure of a translation surface, since both flat and algebro-geometric methods exist to restrict the number of periodic points on a translation surface without knowing the orbit closure. Here is one example.

Theorem 3.12.

Consider a triangle with angles aℓ​π,bℓ​π,cℓ​π\frac{a}{\ell}\pi,\frac{b}{\ell}\pi,\frac{c}{\ell}\pi with ℓ>3\ell>3 prime and {a,b,c}≠{1,2,4}\{a,b,c\}\neq\{1,2,4\}. If two points are finitely blocked they are both vertices and the minimal blocking set is empty in the non-isosceles case and {m}\{m\} where mm is the midpoint of the line joining the two vertices of equal angle in the isosceles case.

Remark 3.13.

The authors have verified that the result still holds for the (1,2,4)(1,2,4) triangle, but have chosen to omit the proof.

Remark 3.14.

We permit billiard paths to run along the edge of the table, but not to pass through vertices of the polygon. Using the description of the finite blocking set, we get moreover that two vertices with different angle are not finitely blocked. The statement allows for the possibility that a vertex is finitely blocked from itself.

If ℓ=3\ell=3, the triangle unfolds to a torus and any two points are finitely blocked.

We require the following deep result due to Tzermias [Tze07, Theorem 1.1] in the nonhyperelliptic case and Grant-Shaulis [GS04, Theorem 1.1] in the hyperelliptic case and which builds on work of Coleman [Col89] and Coleman-Tamagawa-Tzermias [CTT98].

Theorem 3.15.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be the unfolding of a triangle with angles aℓ​π,bℓ​π,cℓ​π\frac{a}{\ell}\pi,\frac{b}{\ell}\pi,\frac{c}{\ell}\pi with ℓ>5\ell>5 prime and so that (a,b,c)≠(1,2,4)(a,b,c)\neq(1,2,4). The only points of (X,ω)(X,\omega) whose difference from a branch point is torsion are branch points and, when (X,ω)(X,\omega) is hyperelliptic, Weierstrass points.

Proof of Theorem 3.12.

By work of Filip, the difference between any two periodic points of (X,ω)(X,\omega) must be torsion in the Jacobian [Fil16a]. (In general, Filip allows for more complicated twisted torsion relations, but to have non-trivial twisting one must consider relations between at least 3 points. In general, Filip also allows for the difference to be merely torsion in a factor of the Jacobian, but since ℓ\ell is prime the relevant factor is in fact the whole Jacobian.)

When ℓ\ell is prime, ω\omega does not lie in any proper rationally defined subspace of H1​(X,ℂ)H^{1}(X,\mathbb{C}), because ω\omega lies in an eigenspace whose Galois conjugates span H1​(X,ℂ)H^{1}(X,\mathbb{C}). It follows that (X,ω)(X,\omega) does not cover a translation surface of smaller genus. So (X,ω)=(Xmin,ωmin)(X,\omega)=(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}). Furthermore, if XX has an involution negating ω\omega, then this involution must be hyperelliptic, since its minus one eigenspace is rationally defined. Hence XX is hyperelliptic or X=QminX=Q_{\operatorname{min}}. By Theorem 3.6 the only pairs of finitely blocked points are points that unfold to periodic points.

Suppose first that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not hyperelliptic. When ℓ>5\ell>5 and {a,b,c}≠{1,2,4}\{a,b,c\}\neq\{1,2,4\}, Theorem 3.15 implies that the only points that unfold to periodic points are vertices of the triangle. By Lemma 3.8, a minimal blocking set of two finitely blocked periodic points consists of only periodic points.

Now suppose (X,ω)(X,\omega) is hyperelliptic. This happens if and only if the triangle is isosceles (see for example [Col89, Section 4]). When ℓ>5\ell>5, Theorem 3.15 states the only points that unfold to periodic points (aside from the vertices) are points that unfold to Weierstrass points. The only such point on an isosceles triangle is the midpoint mm of the edge between the two vertices of equal angle. Indeed, since the hyperelliptic involution is central and is a flat isometry, it descends to an involution of the pillowcase double. (Since ℓ\ell is odd, the hyperelliptic involution cannot be part of the deck group.) This involution can be viewed as an automorphism of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} exchanging two points corresponding to the two equal angles and fixing a third point, and there is only one such involution.

By Lemma 3.8, a minimal blocking set of two finitely blocked periodic points consists of only periodic points. Therefore, mm is not finitely blocked from any of the vertices of the triangle. The trajectories shown in Figure 1 shows that mm is not blocked from itself. Therefore, in the hyperelliptic case we have also shown that the only finitely blocked points are pairs of vertices.

Both triangles with ℓ=5\ell=5 unfold to Teichmüller curves in genus two and hence Möller [Möl06] implies that the only periodic points are zeros and Weierstrass points. Hence the above arguments hold also in this case. ∎

3.4. Description of blocking sets.

Assume that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is not a torus cover.

Theorem 3.16.

Let x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} be finitely blocked on (X,ω)(X,\omega), and let BB be any minimal blocking set. If x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are periodic points, then so are all points in BB. Otherwise, one of the following holds:

  1. (1)

    πXmin​(x1)=πXmin​(x2)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1})=\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{2}), BB does not contain any periodic points and πXmin\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}} maps {x1,x2}∪B\{x_{1},x_{2}\}\cup B to a single point.

  2. (2)

    πXmin​(x1)≠πXmin​(x2)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1})\neq\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{2}) but πQmin​(x1)=πQmin​(x2)\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1})=\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{2}), and if B′B^{\prime} is the set of non-periodic points in BB, then πQmin\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}} maps {x1,x2}∪B′\{x_{1},x_{2}\}\cup B^{\prime} to a single point.

Remark 3.17.

In the case of two periodic points and the case of two points that are identified under πXmin\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}, the converse - i.e. that any such points x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} must be finitely blocked - is false. However, in the third case, the converse follows from Lemma 3.1, which shows that x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are finitely blocked by the preimages under πXmin\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}} of fixed points of the involution on Xm​i​nX_{min}. In particular, a minimal blocking set is contained in the set of periodic points in this case.

Proof of Theorem 3.16.

If both xix_{i} are periodic, the result follows from Lemma 3.8. So assume at least one of x1x_{1} or x2x_{2} is not periodic.

Theorem 3.6 gives that πQmin​(x1)=πQmin​(x2)\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1})=\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{2}), and Lemma 3.8 and Theorem 1.3 give that the blocking sets consists of periodic points and the πQmin\pi_{Q_{\operatorname{min}}} fiber of x1x_{1}. This proves the result if πXmin​(x1)≠πXmin​(x2)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1})\neq\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{2}).

So assume πXmin​(x1)=πXmin​(x2)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1})=\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{2}). Any line segment from x1x_{1} to x2x_{2} maps under πXmin\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}} to a periodic line on (Xmin,ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}). Moving x1x_{1} slightly, we can assume that πXmin​(x1)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1}) is not on the central core curve of any cylinder. Hence any image of πXmin​(x1)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1}) under the involution is not on one of these periodic lines through πXmin​(x1)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1}), so we may assume that B′B^{\prime} maps to πXmin​(x1)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1}). (By Theorem 1.3, every point of B′B^{\prime} maps to either πXmin​(x1)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1}) or its image under the involution (if there is an involution)).

Similarly, moving πXmin​(x1)\pi_{X_{\operatorname{min}}}(x_{1}) slightly we can assume it does not lie on any of the countably many periodic lines through periodic points on (Xmin,ωmin)(X_{\operatorname{min}},\omega_{\operatorname{min}}), and so we get that BB contains no periodic points. ∎

For developments on the illumination and finite blocking problems subsequent to the completion of the present paper, see [AW, Wol].

4. Background

Here we recall some background that will be used in the rest of the paper.

4.1. Affine invariant submanifolds.

Given an affine invariant submanifold ℳ\mathcal{M} and a point (X,ω)(X,\omega) in ℳ\mathcal{M} the tangent space11 1 Formally, an affine invariant submanifold is a properly immersed submanifold in the stratum, and the image of this immersion may have self-crossings. At such a self-crossing, the tangent space depends on not just the surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) in the stratum but also a point in the abstract manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. See [LNW17] for more details. For notational simplicity we will use notation adapted to the case when the image of ℳ\mathcal{M} has no self-crossings and hence ℳ\mathcal{M} can be identified with its image in the stratum. T(X,ω)​ℳT_{(X,\omega)}\mathcal{M} is naturally identified with a subspace of H1​(X,Σ,ℂ)H^{1}(X,\Sigma;\mathbb{C}) where Σ\Sigma is the zero set of ω\omega. Let p:H1​(X,Σ,ℂ)→H1​(X,ℂ)p:H^{1}(X,\Sigma;\mathbb{C})\to H^{1}(X;\mathbb{C}) be the natural map from relative to absolute cohomology. The rank of ℳ\mathcal{M} is defined as rank⁡(ℳ)=12​dimℂp⁡(T(X,ω)​ℳ)\rank(\mathcal{M})=\frac{1}{2}\dim_{\mathbb{C}}p(T_{(X,\omega)}\mathcal{M}) for any (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M}. This is an integer by work of Avila-Eskin-Möller [AEM17].

The affine field of definition 𝐤⁡(ℳ){\mathbf{k}}(\mathcal{M}) of ℳ\mathcal{M} is the smallest subfield of ℝ\mathbb{R} such that ℳ\mathcal{M} can locally be defined by linear equations in period coordinates with coefficients in this field [Wri14]. It is an algebraic extension of ℚ\mathbb{Q} of degree at most deg⁡(𝐤⁡(ℳ))≤g\deg({\mathbf{k}}(\mathcal{M}))\leq g, where gg is the genus.

We will use the matrices

ut=(1t01),at=(100et),rt=(cos⁡(t)−sin⁡(t)sin⁡(t)cos⁡(t)).u_{t}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&t\\ 0&1\end{array}\right),\quad\quad a_{t}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\ 0&e^{t}\end{array}\right),\quad\quad r_{t}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\cos(t)&-\sin(t)\\ \sin(t)&\cos(t)\end{array}\right).

We will refer to a cylinder on a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) together with a choice of orientation of its core curve as an oriented cylinder. Given a collection of parallel oriented cylinders, we will say they are consistently oriented if the holonomies of ω\omega along the oriented core curves are positive multiples of each other.

Given an oriented cylinder CC on a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega), we define utC​(X,ω)u_{t}^{C}(X,\omega) and atC​(X,ω)a_{t}^{C}(X,\omega) to be the result of the following process. Rotate (X,ω)(X,\omega) so that CC becomes horizontal and the orientation is in the positive real direction, apply utu_{t} or ata_{t} respectively to just CC and not to the rest of the surface, and then apply the inverse rotation. Given a collection 𝒞={C1,…,Ck}\mathcal{C}=\{C_{1},\ldots,C_{k}\} of parallel consistently oriented cylinders, define ut𝒞(X,ω)=utC1∘⋯∘utCk(X,ω)u_{t}^{\mathcal{C}}(X,\omega)=u_{t}^{C_{1}}\circ\cdots\circ u_{t}^{C_{k}}(X,\omega) and at𝒞(X,ω)=atC1∘⋯∘atCk(X,ω)a_{t}^{\mathcal{C}}(X,\omega)=a_{t}^{C_{1}}\circ\cdots\circ a_{t}^{C_{k}}(X,\omega). We refer to ut𝒞u_{t}^{\mathcal{C}} as the cylinder shear and at𝒞a_{t}^{\mathcal{C}} as the cylinder stretch. Typically, either a choice of orientation for the cylinders will be clear, or else either choice will be equally good.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be an affine invariant submanifold. We say that two cylinders C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} on a surface (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M} are ℳ\mathcal{M}-parallel if they are parallel and remain parallel on nearby22 2 If ℳ\mathcal{M} has self-crossings, then one considers only deformations arising from a neighbourhood in the abstract manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. surfaces in ℳ\mathcal{M}. These definitions were introduced in [Wri15], where the following is shown.

Theorem 4.1 (Cylinder Deformation Theorem).

If 𝒞\mathcal{C} is an equivalence class of ℳ\mathcal{M}-parallel cylinders on (X,ω)∈ℳ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M}, then ut𝒞∘as𝒞​(X,ω)∈ℳu_{t}^{\mathcal{C}}\circ a_{s}^{\mathcal{C}}(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{M} for all s,t∈ℝs,t\in\mathbb{R}.

If 𝒞\mathcal{C} is as above and contains a saddle connection perpendicular to the core curves, we define the “collapse” of 𝒞\mathcal{C} to be the limit of as𝒞​(X,ω)a_{s}^{\mathcal{C}}(X,\omega) as s→−∞s\to-\infty. The condition that 𝒞\mathcal{C} contains a perpendicular saddle connection connection is equivalent to the surface degenerating as t→−∞t\to-\infty, and here we take the limit in the partial compactification described in [MW17]. If there is a unique t0t_{0} (up to Dehn twists) so that ut0𝒞​(X,ω)u_{t_{0}}^{\mathcal{C}}(X,\omega) contains a saddle connection in 𝒞\mathcal{C} perpendicular to the core curves, for example if 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a single simple cylinder, then we define the cylinder collapse to be the limit of as𝒞​ut0𝒞​(X,ω)a_{s}^{\mathcal{C}}u_{t_{0}}^{\mathcal{C}}(X,\omega) as s→−∞s\to-\infty. (Recall a simple cylinder is one for which each boundary is a single saddle connection.)

Cylinder deformations apply equally well to translations surfaces (X,ω,S)(X,\omega,S) with marked points SS. If we write

(X′,ω′,S′)=lims→−∞as𝒞​(X,ω,S),(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime},S^{\prime})=\lim_{s\to-\infty}a_{s}^{\mathcal{C}}(X,\omega,S),

then the set S′S^{\prime} may have a different size than SS. In particular, S′S^{\prime} maybe be non-empty even when SS is empty [MW17]. In general, (X′,ω′,S′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime},S^{\prime}) might also have multiple components, however in all instances in this paper it will have only a single component.

4.2. Finiteness of periodic points.

We now explain why Theorem 1.2 is a special case of results in [EFW18]. All theorems in [EFW18] apply to affine invariant submanifolds in ℋ∗n\mathcal{H}^{*n}, as well as those in strata without marked points. If 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point, it is in particular an affine invariant submanifold of ℳ∗1\mathcal{M}^{*1} (the preimage of ℳ\mathcal{M} in ℋ∗1\mathcal{H}^{*1}). All of ℳ,ℳ∗1,\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M}^{*1}, and 𝒩\mathcal{N} have the same rank. By assumption, we have that ℳ∗1\mathcal{M}^{*1} is either higher rank (i.e. rank greater than 1) or that the degree of affine field of definition is greater than 1 (or both), since otherwise ℳ\mathcal{M} would consist of torus covers. By [EFW18, Theorem 1.5], such an affine invariant submanifold cannot properly contain infinitely many affine invariant submanifolds of the same rank.

4.3. Strata of quadratic differentials.

Lemma 4.2.

Let 𝒬⁡(κ)\mathcal{Q}(\kappa) where κ=(k1,…,kn)\kappa=(k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}) be a stratum of quadratic differentials. Let mo​d​dm_{odd} be the number of odd numbers in κ\kappa and me​v​e​nm_{even} the number of even numbers. Let gg be the genus of the Riemann surfaces on which the quadratic differentials lie. The rank and rel of the component is then

rk⁡(𝒬)=g+mo​d​d2−1andrel⁡(𝒬)=me​v​e​n.\mathrm{rk}(\mathcal{Q})=g+\frac{m_{odd}}{2}-1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathrm{rel}(\mathcal{Q})=m_{even}.

We define the rel to be the dimension minus twice the rank.

Proof sketch.

The rank is the difference of the genera of surfaces in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and their double covers, which can be computed using Riemann-Hurwitz formula. See [KZ03, Section 2.1] for the formula for dim𝒬\dim\mathcal{Q}. ∎

Corollary 4.3.

The only rank one strata of strictly quadratic differentials are 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), 𝒬⁡(2,−12)\mathcal{Q}(2,-1^{2}), and 𝒬⁡(22)\mathcal{Q}(2^{2}).

4.4. Hat homologous saddle connections.

Two saddle connections or cylinders on (Q,q)∈𝒬(Q,q)\in\mathcal{Q} are called hat homologous if they are parallel and remain so on all nearby surfaces in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. Configurations of hat homologous saddle connections were classified in [MZ08]; in particular, two hat homologous cylinders must have ratio of lengths in {12,1,2}\{\frac{1}{2},1,2\}.

We say that a quadratic differential is generic in a given direction if any two saddle connections in that direction are hat homologous. A cylinder in a half-translation surface is an isometric map of ℝ/(c​ℤ)×(0,h)\mathbb{R}/(c\mathbb{Z})\times(0,h) into the surface. This always extends to a continuous map of ℝ/(c​ℤ)×[0,h]\mathbb{R}/(c\mathbb{Z})\times[0,h] into the surface. The two boundary components of the cylinder are the images of ℝ/(c​ℤ)×{0}\mathbb{R}/(c\mathbb{Z})\times\{0\} and ℝ/(c​ℤ)×{h}\mathbb{R}/(c\mathbb{Z})\times\{h\}. The multiplicity of a saddle connection on the component of the boundary corresponding to ℝ/(c​ℤ)×{0}\mathbb{R}/(c\mathbb{Z})\times\{0\} is the number of preimages of a point in this saddle connection in ℝ/(c​ℤ)×{0}\mathbb{R}/(c\mathbb{Z})\times\{0\}, and similarly for ℝ/(c​ℤ)×{h}\mathbb{R}/(c\mathbb{Z})\times\{h\}. This multiplicity is always 1 or 2. Define a simple cylinder to be one that has one saddle connection, with multiplicity one, in each of its boundaries.

We recall the following consequences of [MZ08, Theorems 1 and 2].

Proposition 4.4.

Suppose that CC is a cylinder in a generic direction on a quadratic differential. Then each boundary component of CC consists of either

  1. (1)

    one saddle connection with multiplicity one,

  2. (2)

    one saddle connection with multiplicity two, or

  3. (3)

    two saddle connections, each with multiplicity one.

In the last case, removing the two saddle connections disconnects the surface, and the component not containing CC has trivial linear holonomy.

Furthermore if CC shares a boundary saddle connection with another cylinder C′C^{\prime}, then possibly after switching CC and C′C^{\prime} we have that C′C^{\prime} is simple and does not share a boundary saddle connection with any other cylinder, and CC has two saddle connections in the given boundary component as in case (3) above.

4.5. Primitivity

A half-translation covering map from a quadratic differential (Q,q)(Q,q) to a quadratic differential (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) is defined to be a branched covering f:Q→Q′f:Q\to Q^{\prime} of Riemann surfaces such that q=f∗​(q′)q=f^{*}(q^{\prime}). So the definition is essentially identical to the definition of translation covering map, but the word “half” reminds us that the domain might not be an Abelian differential.

Lemma 4.5.

The generic element of a component of a stratum of Abelian or quadratic differentials admits a non-bijective half-translation cover to another translation or half-translation surface if and only if the component is hyperelliptic. If the component is hyperelliptic and has rank bigger than 1, then the quotient by the hyperelliptic involution is the only such map.

This is related to, but stronger than, [Möl09, Theorem 1.1]. Since we are not aware of a proof of the lemma in the literature, we sketch one way that the lemma can be verified.

Proof.

All rank 1 strata are hyperelliptic, so we assume the stratum has rank at least 2. In particular, the generic surface in the stratum doesn’t cover a surface in 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}).

Suppose the generic element (Q,q)(Q,q) of a stratum 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is a cover of (Q0,q0)∈𝒬0≠𝒬⁡(−14)(Q_{0},q_{0})\in\mathcal{Q}_{0}\neq\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}) of degree d>1d>1. It follows that every element of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is a cover of a surface in 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0}.

We define an envelope to be a cylinder that has one boundary that consists of one saddle connection of multiplicity two; see Figure 2. An envelope is simple if it also has one boundary that only contains a multiplicity one saddle connection.

We first claim d=2d=2. It is possible to find a surface (Q0,q0)∈𝒬0(Q_{0},q_{0})\in\mathcal{Q}_{0} with a cylinder C0C_{0} that is a simple cylinder or a simple envelope; for example, this follows from Lemma 6.1. We can assume that C0C_{0} doesn’t contain any branch points by simply moving them out of C0C_{0}.

In particular C0C_{0} has a zero (that isn’t a pole) on at least one side. That side must consists of a single multiplicity one saddle connection, and its preimage consists of dd saddle connections of the same length.

Suppose first that C0C_{0} is a simple cylinder. In that case, there can’t be more than one cylinder in the preimage, because cylinders in the preimage must have equal height and generic surfaces in a stratum don’t have cylinders of the same height. So we get that the preimage is a single cylinder. This single cylinder has dd saddle connections on each side, giving d=2d=2 by Proposition 4.4.

The case where C0C_{0} isn’t simple is a bit more subtle because a component of the preimage of C0C_{0} can have twice the height of C0C_{0}. Using the arguments from before we reduce to the case where the preimage has one component, and is twice the height and twice the circumference, with two saddle connections on each side. Let C′C^{\prime} be any cylinder in the complement of the preimage. By Proposition 4.4, it can be seen to be simple. Repeating the argument using the image of C′C^{\prime} in the place of C0C_{0} completes the proof that d=2d=2.

Given d=2d=2, the lemma follows from a Riemann-Hurwitz argument, using that if the generic element of one stratum covers an element of another, the dimension of the first stratum must be at least as large as the second, as in the determination of which strata have a hyperelliptic component [KZ03, Lan04]. ∎

Remark 4.6.

Given Corollary 4.3, Lemma 4.5 implies that the only genus 00 stratum where every surface has an involution is 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}). Lemma 4.5 (plus a direct verification in 𝒬⁡(2,2)\mathcal{Q}(2,2) and 𝒬⁡(2,−12)\mathcal{Q}(2,-1^{2})) shows that in every hyperelliptic stratum other than 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}) and ℋ⁡(∅)\mathcal{H}(\emptyset), the hyperelliptic involution is unique on a generic surface. (In genus zero or genus one a surface can have several hyperelliptic involutions.)

5. Proof of Theorem 1.4

Throughout the rest of this paper, 𝒬,𝒬′\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}, etc., will denote connected components of strata of quadratic differentials. Recall that point markings over strata of Abelian differentials are classified in [Api20], so we make the following standing assumption for the remainder of the paper.

Assumption 5.1.

All strata of quadratic differentials considered will not consist of squares of Abelian differentials.

We begin by noting that we have already classified irreducible nn-point markings with n>1n>1, as a consequence of Theorem 1.3 and Lemma 4.5.

Corollary 5.2.

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} have rank bigger than 1. If 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not hyperelliptic, then there are no irreducible nn-point markings with n>1n>1. If 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is hyperelliptic, the only such point markings occur when n=2n=2 and the two points are interchanged by the involution.

Recall that, by Corollary 4.3, the first requirement simply says that 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), 𝒬⁡(2,−12)\mathcal{Q}(2,-1^{2}), or 𝒬⁡(22)\mathcal{Q}(2^{2}).

Proof.

One can rephrase Lemma 4.5 as saying that if (Q,q)(Q,q) is a generic element of a non-hyperelliptic 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, then (Qmin,qmin)=(Q,q)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}})=(Q,q), and otherwise (Qmin,qmin)(Q_{\operatorname{min}},q_{\operatorname{min}}) is the quotient by the hyperelliptic involution. ∎
