The following proposition will provide the inductive step for our arguments. Recall that an envelope is a cylinder that has one boundary that consists of one saddle connection of multiplicity two. An envelope is simple if it also has one boundary that only contains a multiplicity one saddle connection.

In regards to Assumption 5.1, we remark that degenerating a simple cylinder or a simple envelope on a quadratic differential with non-trivial holonomy will not create a quadratic differential with trivial holonomy. (In contrast, degenerating a non-simple envelope may create a quadratic differential with trivial linear holonomy.)

Proposition 5.3.

Suppose that (Q,q)∈𝒬(Q,q)\in\mathcal{Q} has a simple cylinder CC, and that degenerating CC gives (Q′,q′,S)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime},S), where (Q′,q′)∈𝒬′(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} and 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} does not have any periodic points. Then 𝒬\mathcal{Q} does not have any periodic points.

The same conclusion holds if (Q,q)(Q,q) has a disjoint pair of simple envelopes, and degenerating either one similarly gives a 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} without periodic points.

We will defer this proof of Proposition 5.3 to the end of the section. A periodic point for a stratum of quadratic differential is a point marking of the same dimension, as in the case of Abelian differential. Each periodic point for 𝒬\mathcal{Q} can be lifted to one for 𝒬~\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}. (The fibers of the periodic point double in size, and we do not comment on whether the new periodic point is irreducible.)

In the next two sections we will prove the following two results, which we will use in our proof of Theorem 1.4. Note that the three strata that appear in the next theorem are exactly the higher rank strata of minimal dimension (they have dimension 4 and rank 2), and that all rank 1 strata are hyperelliptic.

Theorem 5.4.

If 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is non-hyperelliptic, and

𝒬∉{𝒬⁡(3,−13),𝒬⁡(5,−1),𝒬⁡(1,−15)},\mathcal{Q}\notin\{\mathcal{Q}(3,-1^{3}),\mathcal{Q}(5,-1),\mathcal{Q}(1,-1^{5})\},

then there exists (Q,q)∈𝒬(Q,q)\in\mathcal{Q} with a simple cylinder, or a pair of disjoint simple envelopes, such that degenerating any one of these cylinders gives (Q′,q′,S)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime},S), where (Q′,q′)∈𝒬′(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} and 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} is non-hyperelliptic.

Theorem 5.5.

𝒬⁡(3,−13),𝒬⁡(5,−1)\mathcal{Q}(3,-1^{3}),\mathcal{Q}(5,-1) and 𝒬⁡(1,−15)\mathcal{Q}(1,-1^{5}) do not have periodic points.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

By using induction on dim𝒬\dim\mathcal{Q}, Proposition 5.3 and Theorems 5.4 and 5.5 immediately give the result when 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not hyperelliptic.

When 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is hyperelliptic, every surface in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} covers a surface in a genus 0 stratum 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0}, which is not hyperelliptic and has the same rank. Let nn be the number of points that are not zeros or poles over which these covering maps are branched. (One can show n∈{0,1,2}n\in\{0,1,2\}.) Any 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-periodic point gives rise to a periodic point over 𝒬0∗n\mathcal{Q}_{0}^{*n}. This can be considered as a point marking over 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0}, and in this point marking the point arising from the 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-periodic point is not free. By Corollary 5.2 this means we get a 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0}-periodic point, which is a contradiction. ∎

Remark 5.6.

Theorem 5.4 is false without Assumption 5.1. Namely, if 𝒬=ℋo​d​d​(4)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{H}^{odd}(4), then 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not hyperelliptic, but every degeneration of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is a genus two stratum of Abelian differentials and hence hyperelliptic. Thus our proof does not apply as written to strata of Abelian differentials.

However, a variant of the proof of Theorem 5.4 shows that in a connected component of a stratum of Abelian differentials of genus at least 3 other than ℋo​d​d​(4)\mathcal{H}^{odd}(4) there is a surface with a simple cylinder that may be degenerated to produce a translation surface in a nonhyperelliptic connected component. A new proof of the classification of periodic points for Abelian differentials then follows almost verbatim to the proof for quadratic differentials. We omit the arguments for Abelian differentials.

Now we will proceed with the proof of Proposition 5.3. The difficulty of the proof is that if we naively collapse CC, it may be that as CC decreases in size, the periodic point converges to a zero or pole, so that on the limit there is no periodic point. Notice that the assumptions imply that 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not rank one.

Proof of Proposition 5.3.

We will handle both cases simultaneously. In the first case, CC is the given simple cylinder, and in the second case, we let CC be either envelope. Suppose to a contradiction that pp is a 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-periodic point on (Q,q)(Q,q). Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the equivalence class of cylinders 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-parallel to CC, and suppose without loss of generality that 𝒞\mathcal{C} consists of horizontal cylinders and that the horizontal direction is generic. Our analysis will place increasingly strong constraints on pp, until eventually we reach a contradiction.

Suppose without loss of generality, after shearing the surface, that CC contains a vertical saddle connection. Recall we have defined the collapse of CC to be the limit of asC​(Q,q)a_{s}^{C}(Q,q) as s→−∞s\to-\infty. Here it will be important that this limit can be thought of as limit of the path alog⁡(t)C​(Q,q)a_{\log(t)}^{C}(Q,q), which is linear in period coordinates as tt ranges from ee to 00. We refer to this whole path as the collapse path of CC.

The proof will proceed in three steps. First, we will show that it suffices to show that we can move the marked point out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Second, we will show that if we can’t collapse CC without pp merging with a singularity then the position of pp is entirely controlled by CC, in a precise sense specified at the beginning of step 2. Finally, we will show that if the position of pp is entirely controlled by CC then pp can be moved out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Step 1: pp must belong to a cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We claim that if pp is not contained in the interior or boundary of a cylinder of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, then its position in the complement of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is unchanged by any cylinder deformation of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. To see this, first slightly change the heights of 𝒞\mathcal{C} so there is no rational relation between the moduli of the cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. By the Cylinder Deformation Theorem (Theorem 4.1), we know we can equally twist the cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C} without changing the position of pp. It follows from one of the easiest ingredients in the proof of Theorem 4.1, namely [Wri15, Corollary 3.4], that we can individually twist each cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C} without changing the position of pp, because this twist is a limit of the deformations of 𝒞\mathcal{C} guaranteed to exist by the Cylinder Deformation Theorem. See also [MW17, Lemma 4.6]. The claim is proved.

Hence, if pp is disjoint from the closure of the cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we may collapse CC and pass to a boundary surface (Q′,q′,S∪{p})(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime},S\cup\{p\}), where (Q′,q′)∈𝒬′(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} and 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} does not have any periodic points. Mirzakhani-Wright [MW17] gives that p∈(Q′,q′,S∪{p})p\in(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime},S\cup\{p\}) is not free, and by assumption pp cannot be a 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} periodic point. But since 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} does not have periodic points, 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} cannot be hyperelliptic, so Corollary 5.2 implies that pp is either free or a 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}-periodic point, giving a contradiction.

Suppose now that pp lies on the boundary of CC for all time as CC collapses. Then we proceed as follows. If CC is a simple cylinder, then we proceed with the collapse and arrive at the same contradiction as before. If CC is an envelope, then it may not be possible to collapse CC without causing pp to coincide with a singularity on the boundary, see Figure 4 (bottom). In this case, we relabel the cylinders so that the second envelope is labeled CC. (This is why we require two envelopes.)

The proof is similar but easier if pp is on the boundary of another cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C} for all time as CC collapses.

Step 2: CC determines the position of pp.

We may now suppose that pp is contained in the interior of a cylinder D∈𝒞D\in\mathcal{C}, and either D=CD=C or the position of pp in the complement of CC is not constant along the collapse path. We will show that we may assume that there is a saddle connection joining pp to a zero on the boundary of DD whose holonomy is a fixed real multiple of a cross curve of CC. We will also show C≠DC\neq D. Thus, this step could be more completely described as “D≠CD\neq C, and CC determines the position of pp in DD.”

Shear (Q,q)(Q,q) so that pp does not lie on a vertical separatrix (this could easily cause CC to no longer contain a vertical saddle connection). Recall the collapse path is defined to start at t=et=e and end at t=0t=0. Because we have assumed pp does not lie on a vertical separatrix, pp does not hit a singularity of the metric before t=0t=0. We may partition the interval (0,e)(0,e) into closed subintervals according to which cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C} (including the boundary of the cylinder) pp is in at a given time t∈(0,e)t\in(0,e). (The subintervals overlap at their endpoints, and by convention we require adjacent intervals to correspond to distinct cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.)

Let γ\gamma be a path from a singularity to the periodic point. Let f⁡(t)f(t) denote the imaginary part of the period of γ\gamma at time tt along the collapse path. (The function ff is only well defined up to replacing it with −f-f). If hh is the height of the shortest cylinder in 𝒞−{C}\mathcal{C}-\{C\}, then pp passes through at most |f⁡(0)−f⁡(e)|h\frac{|f(0)-f(e)|}{h} cylinders in 𝒞−{C}\mathcal{C}-\{C\} along the collapse path. This shows that the partition described in the previous paragraph is finite.

By replacing (Q,q)(Q,q) with an appropriate point on the collapse path, we may assume that in fact pp remains in DD along the collapse path. Giving up our assumption that pp doesn’t lie on a vertical separatrix, with can replace (Q,q)(Q,q) with a sheared version of itself to again assume without loss of generality that the cylinder CC contains a vertical saddle connection v1v_{1}. Note that the assumption that pp remains in DD is still valid.

Suppose first that C=DC=D. If pp lies on a vertical separatrix contained in CC then we may shear the surface to perform a full Dehn twist (in the case that CC is simple) or half a Dehn twist (in the case that CC is an envelope) to ensure that CC still contains a vertical saddle connection and that pp does not lie on a vertical separatrix contained in CC. See Figure 4 and, for a non-example, Figure 5. Collapsing CC now gives a half translation surface where pp is not a singularity of the metric, but is a periodic point, which is a contradiction.

Next we suppose that C≠DC\neq D. Suppose that there is a small perturbation of (Q,q)(Q,q), so that v1v_{1} remains vertical and CC remains horizontal, and such that after replacing (Q,q)(Q,q) with this deformation pp does not collide with a singularity at the conclusion of the collapse path. If this occurs, then, as above, pp becomes a periodic point on the boundary, which has no periodic points by hypothesis. Therefore, we may suppose that after any small perturbation as above, pp collides with a singularity at the conclusion of the collapse path. In particular, this means that there is a saddle connection v2v_{2} in DD joining a singularity on the boundary of DD to pp, and a positive real constant cc, so that the orbit closure of (Q,q,p)(Q,q;p) locally satisfies the equation v2=c​v1v_{2}=cv_{1}.

Step 3: pp may be moved out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

The idea of the proof will now be to vary v1v_{1} to move the periodic point pp outside of 𝒞\mathcal{C} (which will be a contradiction). Since v2=c​v1v_{2}=cv_{1} we see that by shearing CC to the left or right while fixing the complement of CC we may move the marked point to the left or right. Similarly, increasing the height of CC while fixing the rest of the surface causes pp to move up or down. We will use these two operations to force pp to move through the complement of CC (and we will be careful not to cause pp to enter CC). We will refer in the sequel to these operations as “moving pp using CC”. Suppose that increasing the height of CC moves pp toward a boundary BB of DD.

Our approach will use the results of Masur-Zorich [MZ08] that we summarized in Proposition 4.4. In the sequel, we will say that a saddle connection “leads out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}” if it borders a cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C} on exactly one side.

Sublemma 5.7.

The boundary BB cannot contain two saddle connections of multiplicity one.

Proof.

Suppose not to a contradiction. If both saddle connections in BB lead out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} then we increase the height of CC to move pp through BB and out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Otherwise, by Proposition 4.4 the boundary BB of DD is as in one of the subfigures in Figure 6

We see that the left two configurations are impossible, as shown in Figure 7. In that figure, we shear CC and increase its height so that the marked point leaves 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In the right configuration of Figure 7 this is easy since there is a saddle connection b0b_{0} in BB that leads out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In the left configuration one of the two simple cylinders bordering BB, call it EE, is not CC, and passing through EE leads out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} by Proposition 4.4.

Therefore, DD and its boundary BB are arranged as in Figure 8. Let D′D^{\prime} be the simple cylinder that borders DD along BB.

Let B′B^{\prime} be the boundary of DD opposite BB. Notice that B′B^{\prime} cannot consist of a single multiplicity two saddle connection since then 𝒬=𝒬⁡(2,−12)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}(2,-1^{2}), which is rank one. Moreover, B′B^{\prime} cannot consist of two multiplicity one saddle connections that bound a simple cylinder (as in Figure 8) since then 𝒬=𝒬⁡(2,2)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}(2,2), which is also rank one. Therefore, Proposition 4.4 implies that either B′B^{\prime} contains a saddle connection that leads out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} or B′B^{\prime} borders two distinct simple cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The possibilities are shown in Figure 9. In that figure we see that when D′≠CD^{\prime}\neq C it is possible to shear CC and increase its height to move the marked point pp out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as we did in Figure 7. It is important that D′≠CD^{\prime}\neq C since the marked point will pass through D′D^{\prime} as it moves to leave 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

Therefore, we may suppose that D′=CD^{\prime}=C. Recall that there is a cross curve v1v_{1} in CC and a positive real constant cc so that v2=c​v1v_{2}=cv_{1} where v2v_{2} is a saddle connection joining a singularity on B′B^{\prime} to pp. We now decrease the height of CC so that the imaginary part of the period of v1v_{1} changes from positive to negative. As we see in Figure 10, this “overcollapse of CC” can be performed in a way that moves the marked point out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} (in the rightmost figure we must first make the bottom cylinder that the marked point passes through sufficiently small; this may be achieved without affecting the position of the marked point since v2=c​v1v_{2}=cv_{1}).

When CC overcollapses, a new horizontal cylinder C′C^{\prime} is created, visible at the top of the figures in Figure 10. It is simple, with both boundary components glued to the cylinder D∈𝒞D\in\mathcal{C} below it, so it is generically parallel to the surviving cylinders of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. (One might say more informally that C′C^{\prime} is “in 𝒞\mathcal{C}”, meaning that it is in the equivalence class of the surviving cylinders of 𝒞\mathcal{C}.) No other horizontal cylinders are created by the overcollapse, since it does not effect the rest of the surface.

Once pp has left 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we obtain a contradiction as follows. After CC is collapsed, the continuation of the overcollapse deformation of the unmarked surface is actually a cylinder deformation of C′C^{\prime} and DD; more precisely it increases the height of C′C^{\prime} and decreases the height of DD. Since both C′C^{\prime} and DD are in the equivalence class of the surviving cylinders in 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and since the marked point is now not contained in the closure of this equivalence class, this contradicts the initial claim in Step 1. ∎

Sublemma 5.8.

The cylinder DD is simple and borders an equivalent cylinder along BB.

Proof.

Suppose first to a contradiction that BB consists of one multiplicity two saddle connection. By Proposition 4.4 we have that DD must look like one of the cylinders in Figure 11.

The leftmost configuration only occurs in 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), which is rank one and hence precluded. In the middle configuration the boundary B′B^{\prime} opposite BB is a single multiplicity one saddle connection, which must lead out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} by Proposition 4.4. Therefore, increasing the height of CC moves the marked point through BB and then out the opposite boundary of DD and hence out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In the rightmost configuration we increase the height of CC to move the marked point through BB and then into a situation where as the height of CC increases the marked point moves towards a boundary with two multiplicity one saddle connections. As in Sublemma 5.7, specifically Figure 7, one of these saddle connections either leads out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} or borders a cylinder other than CC, which in turn leads out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, so we reach a contradiction.

By Sublemma 5.7, BB cannot consist of two multiplicity one saddle connections. Therefore, by Proposition 4.4, it must consist of a single multiplicity one saddle connection. If BB does not border another cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C} then by increasing the height of CC we may move the marked point through BB and out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, which is a contradiction (see the rightmost figure in Figure 7 for a similar case). Therefore, BB borders another cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C} and hence by Proposition 4.4, DD is simple. ∎

Let D′D^{\prime} be the other cylinder in 𝒞\mathcal{C} which borders BB. Because CC is a simple cylinder or a simple envelope, D′≠CD^{\prime}\neq C. As pp moves into D′D^{\prime} it moves towards a boundary B′′B^{\prime\prime} of D′D^{\prime}. We will reach a contradiction by moving pp out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Since all argument are very similar to those already given in this step, we will only sketch them here.

If B′′B^{\prime\prime} consists of one multiplicity two saddle connection then we proceed as in the middle left subfigure of Figure 12.

If B′′B^{\prime\prime} borders a simple cylinder on both boundaries then call this cylinder D′′D^{\prime\prime}. If D′′=CD^{\prime\prime}=C then we may reduce the height of CC to move pp out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as in the leftmost subfigure of Figure 12 (if there is another cylinder bordering D′D^{\prime} then we first make it short so that we do not need to overcollapse CC to move pp out of 𝒞\mathcal{C}). Otherwise, we move pp out of 𝒞\mathcal{C} as in middle right subfigure of Figure 12. In all other cases we proceed as in the rightmost subfigure of Figure 12. ∎

6. Proof of Theorem 5.4

To read this section it is necessary to be comfortable with the results of [MZ08] that are recalled in Proposition 4.4. Assumption 5.1 is still in effect; otherwise 𝒬=ℋo​d​d​(4)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{H}^{odd}(4) would be a counterexample to Theorem 5.4.

Lemma 6.1.

Any 𝒬\mathcal{Q} other than 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}) contains a surface with a simple cylinder or two disjoint simple envelopes.

Proof.

Pick disjoint cylinders C,DC,D on a surface in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} where all parallel saddle connections are hat homologous. If both are simple envelopes, or if either is a simple cylinder, we are done, so we assume otherwise. In particular, assume CC is not a simple envelope or a simple cylinder.

By Proposition 4.4, since CC is not a simple envelope and is not a simple cylinder, it has exactly two distinct saddle connections on at least one side, and cutting these saddle connections disconnects the surface into two components. Furthermore, the component RR not containing CC has trivial holonomy.

If RR contains a cylinder C′C^{\prime} hat homologous to CC, then C′C^{\prime} must be simple. Otherwise, [SW04] gives a cylinder C′C^{\prime} on RR not parallel to CC, which must be simple.

(The use of [SW04] can be avoided by an argument using square-tiled surfaces. The use of translation surface with boundary can be avoided by gluing together the two boundary saddle connections of RR. We are using the fact that on a generic Abelian differential, every cylinder is simple.) ∎

Lemma 6.2.

Suppose (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) is in a hyperelliptic component other than 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), SS is a set of non-singular points of the metric, and cc is a saddle connection on (Q′,q′,S)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime},S). Assume all points of SS are endpoints of cc (so |S|∈{0,1,2}|S|\in\{0,1,2\}). Then, possibly after moving (Q′,q′,S)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime},S) in its stratum in such a way that cc remains a saddle connection, there is a simple cylinder C′C^{\prime} on (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) disjoint from cc and that does not contain any point of SS on its boundary.

Proof.

We assume all parallel saddle connections on (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) are hat homologous. Notice that since 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is a hyperelliptic component no cylinder is a simple envelope since every cylinder must be fixed by the hyperelliptic involution and a simple envelope does not admit an involution.

First suppose SS is non-empty. Keeping in mind that the surface does not contain simple envelopes, Lemma 6.1 gives a cylinder C′C^{\prime} as desired, except that it may not be disjoint from cc. However, moving the marked points we may make cc disjoint from C′C^{\prime}. (Note that since C′C^{\prime} is simple it cannot cover the whole surface.)

So assume SS is empty. Let C′C^{\prime} be any cylinder disjoint from cc. If C′C^{\prime} is simple we are done. Since the component is hyperelliptic, C′C^{\prime} can’t be a simple envelope, and must have the same number of saddle connections on each of its two boundary components. If C′C^{\prime} has two distinct saddle connections on each side then by Proposition 4.4, C′C^{\prime} disconnects the surface. Cut the two saddle connections on the opposite side from cc. By Proposition 4.4, the component RR not containing C′C^{\prime} or cc has trivial holonomy. As in Lemma 6.1, we can find a simple cylinder in RR.

The case that remains is that every cylinder C′C^{\prime} disjoint from cc is an envelope that has two multiplicity one saddle connections on one boundary. In this case Proposition 4.4 gives that the complement of C′C^{\prime} is connected and has trivial holonomy. In particular, there are only two poles, so we can’t have two disjoint cylinders C′C^{\prime} of this type.

Assume cc is horizontal, and nudge the surface so that it becomes square-tiled. If there is more than one horizontal cylinder, by the previous comment at least one of them must not be as in the previous paragraph, so we obtain a contradiction (after nudging the surface again to restore the fact that all parallel saddle connections are hat homologous). So assume there is just one horizontal cylinder. If a saddle connection other than cc appears both on the top and the bottom of this cylinder, then we can find a transverse simple cylinder disjoint from cc, as in Figure 13 (left). So assume this is not the case. If two distinct saddle connections other than cc appear on the same side of the cylinder, we can nudge them to create a second horizontal cylinder while keeping the existing horizontal cylinder and cc horizontal, as illustrated in Figure 13 (right) in an example. (One can keep the surface horizontally periodic after the nudge by making it still be square-tiled, i.e. have rational period coordinates.)

We are now in one of the four cases illustrated in the top of Figure 14. Except that the left case is in 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}) and hence excluded by our assumption that (Q′,q′)∉𝒬⁡(−14)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime})\notin\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), and the right case is excluded since there is a marked point. For the middle two cases, the bottom of the figure shows how to find a simple cylinder disjoint from cc. ∎

Lemma 6.3.

Let (Q′,q′)∈𝒬′(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}, and assume 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} is hyperelliptic. Let cc be a saddle connection. Let (Q,q)(Q,q) be the quadratic differential that arises from slitting cc and gluing in a simple cylinder. Then (Q,q)(Q,q) belongs to a hyperelliptic component of a stratum of quadratic differentials if and only if cc is fixed by a hyperelliptic involution.

We omit the proof. By Assumption 5.1 and Remark 4.6, the hyperelliptic involution is unique for 𝒬′\mathcal{Q}^{\prime} except when 𝒬′=𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}=\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}). For 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), there are two hyperelliptic involutions.

Lemma 6.4.

Suppose C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are disjoint simple cylinders on (Q,q)(Q,q) such that collapsing either CiC_{i} does not create marked points and gives a surface in a hyperelliptic component. Then (Q,q)(Q,q) is in a hyperelliptic component or 𝒬⁡(5,−1){\mathcal{Q}}(5,-1).

Proof.

Degenerating both CiC_{i} gives a hyperelliptic surface (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) with no marked points and with two saddle connections, c1c_{1} and c2c_{2}. (If marked points were created, then even after moving the marked points in an arbitrary way there would have to be a hyperelliptic involution preserving the set of marked points. By assumption Assumption 5.1, q′q^{\prime} is not the square of a genus 1 Abelian differential. Hence q′q^{\prime} has at least one zero, and hence (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) has at mostly finitely many hyperelliptic involutions (typically only 1!). Hence it is is not possible that the set of marked points is preserved by a hyperelliptic involution even after being moved in an arbitrary way. This contrasts with ℋ⁡(0,0)\mathcal{H}(0,0).)

Since gluing in a cylinder to either cic_{i} gives a surface in a hyperelliptic component, Lemma 6.3 gives that each cic_{i} is fixed by the involution. Hence Lemma 6.3 gives that (Q,q)(Q,q) is hyperelliptic.

This proof works as long as the hyperelliptic involution on (Q′,q′)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime}) is unique, which is true for all strata but 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}) and ℋ⁡(∅)\mathcal{H}(\emptyset), the latter of which cannot arise here. If (Q′,q′)∈𝒬⁡(−14)(Q^{\prime},q^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}), there is the possibility that c1c_{1} is fixed by one hyperelliptic involution, and c2c_{2} by another, as in Figure 15. In this case (Q,q)∈𝒬⁡(5,−1)(Q,q)\in\mathcal{Q}(5,-1). ∎

Proof of Theorem 5.4.

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be non-hyperelliptic and not 𝒬⁡(3,−13),\mathcal{Q}(3,-1^{3}), 𝒬⁡(5,−1)\mathcal{Q}(5,-1), or 𝒬⁡(1,−15)\mathcal{Q}(1,-1^{5}).

Let C1C_{1} be a cylinder that is either simple or a simple envelope on some (Q,q)∈𝒬(Q,q)\in\mathcal{Q}. This exists by Lemma 6.1. If possible, pick C1C_{1} so that degenerating it produces marked points; otherwise we will assume that degenerating any simple cylinder or simple envelope does not produce marked points.

Let (Q1,q1,S1)(Q_{1},q_{1},S_{1}) be the result of degenerating C1C_{1}. The cylinder C1C_{1} becomes a saddle connection c1c_{1} on (Q1,q1,S1)(Q_{1},q_{1},S_{1}). We may assume (Q1,q1)(Q_{1},q_{1}) is in a hyperelliptic component.

Case 1: (Q1,q1)∉𝒬⁡(−14)(Q_{1},q_{1})\notin\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}). Let C2C_{2} be the cylinder on (Q1,q1,S1)(Q_{1},q_{1},S_{1}) given by Lemma 6.2, which is disjoint from c1c_{1}. There is a corresponding cylinder on (Q,q)(Q,q), which we also call C2C_{2}. Let (Q2,q2,S2)(Q_{2},q_{2},S_{2}) be the result of degenerating C2C_{2} on (Q,q)(Q,q). We may assume (Q2,q2)(Q_{2},q_{2}) is in a hyperelliptic component. Since surfaces in hyperelliptic components don’t contain simple envelopes, we get that both CiC_{i} are simple.

We now claim that S1S_{1} is empty. Otherwise, since C2C_{2} does not contain any points of S1S_{1} in its boundary, we see that degenerating C1C_{1} on (Q2,q2)(Q_{2},q_{2}) (with marked points S2S_{2} forgotten) produces a surface with marked points. Since (Q2,q2)(Q_{2},q_{2}) is contained in a hyperelliptic component, every element of the resulting stratum of surfaces with marked points must have an involution fixing the set of marked points. This implies the resulting stratum is ℋ⁡(0,0)\mathcal{H}(0,0), which contradicts Assumption 5.1.

Now assume S1S_{1} is empty. Our choice of C1C_{1} implies that S2S_{2} is empty. Hence Lemma 6.4 contradicts the assumption that 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is non-hyperelliptic.

Case 2: (Q1,q1)∈𝒬⁡(−14)(Q_{1},q_{1})\in\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}). If S1=∅S_{1}=\emptyset, as in Figure 16 we get that C1C_{1} is a simple cylinder, since otherwise (Q,q)∈𝒬⁡(−14,0)(Q,q)\in\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4},0), a contradiction. As in Figure 17 (top left) we conclude that 𝒬=𝒬⁡(2,−1,−1)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}(2,-1,-1). This contradicts our assumption that 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is not hyperelliptic.

If |S1|=2|S_{1}|=2, then C1C_{1} was simple and 𝒬=𝒬⁡(4,−14)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}(4,-1^{4}). See Figure 17 (top right). One can find a pair of disjoint simple envelopes E,E′E,E^{\prime} as in the figure such that degenerating either gives a surface in 𝒬⁡(3,−13)\mathcal{Q}(3,-1^{3}).

If |S1|=1|S_{1}|=1, and C1C_{1} was a simple envelope, then 𝒬=𝒬⁡(1,−15)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}(1,-1^{5}). See Figure 17 (bottom left).

If |S1||S_{1}|=1 and C1C_{1} was simple, 𝒬=𝒬⁡(3,−13)\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}(3,-1^{3}). See Figure 17 (bottom right). ∎

7. Proof of Theorem 5.5

The case of 𝒬⁡(1,−15)\mathcal{Q}(1,-1^{5}) follows from [Api20], which in particular classifies ℋ⁡(2)=𝒬~​(1,−15)\mathcal{H}(2)=\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(1,-1^{5})-periodic points. So we need only treat 𝒬⁡(3,−13)\mathcal{Q}(3,-1^{3}) and 𝒬⁡(5,−1)\mathcal{Q}(5,-1).

Lemma 7.1 (Lemma 5.5 [Api20]).

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a generic translation surface in an affine invariant submanifold ℳ\mathcal{M}. Let CC be a horizontal cylinder, and let 𝒟1,𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2} be two vertical distinct ℳ\mathcal{M}-equivalence classes of cylinders such that the following two conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    The intersection of ∪𝒟i¯\overline{\cup\mathcal{D}_{i}} with the interior of CC is connected and nonempty for i=1,2i=1,2. (Here ∪𝒟1\cup\mathcal{D}_{1} denotes the union of the cylinders in 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}, etc.)

  2. (2)

    Any cylinder equivalent to CC has a modulus that is an integer multiple of the modulus of CC.

If pp is an ℳ\mathcal{M}-periodic point in the interior of CC, then up to relabelling 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2}, the point pp is at the center of the rectangle given by the intersection of ∪𝒟1¯\overline{\cup\mathcal{D}_{1}} and CC. Furthermore, removing ∪𝒟1¯\overline{\cup\mathcal{D}_{1}} and ∪𝒟2¯\overline{\cup\mathcal{D}_{2}} divides CC into two rectangles of equal size.

The lemma allows for multiple intersections of cylinders in 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} and CC, but requires that the union of these intersections be a single rectangle for each ii.

We will apply Lemma 7.1 to the vertically and horizontally periodic surfaces in Figure 19. Note that our convention is that, except where indicated otherwise, opposite edges are identified when giving polygonal presentations for surfaces.

The Cylinder Deformation Theorem implies that these surfaces are generic whenever the ratio of moduli of two inequivalent vertical and horizontal cylinders is irrational. Therefore, identifying the periodic points on these generic surfaces is sufficient to identify the periodic points in the corresponding strata of quadratic differentials.

Periodic points in 𝒬⁡(3,−13)\mathcal{Q}(3,-1^{3}): Consider the surface on the left in Figure 19. Letting CC be either the top or bottom horizontal cylinder, and 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2} be the two equivalence classes of vertical cylinders, Lemma 7.1 implies that any periodic point contained in one of these two horizontal cylinders must be at the points indicated with solid dots. Letting CC be the middle vertical cylinder and 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2} be the two equivalence classes of horizontal cylinders, Lemma 7.1 implies that any periodic point in CC must at the points indicated with circles. Since any of the solid dots can be moved into the middle vertical cylinder by a Dehn twist in horizontal cylinders, the solid dots are not periodic points (since they don’t move onto circled points). The Dehn twist is possible by the Cylinder Deformation Theorem.

Note the three cylinders labelled CC in the preceding paragraph cover the whole surface except for vertical saddle connection in the middle vertical cylinder and two horizontal saddle connections on the top and bottom horizontal cylinder. However, a point on these saddle connections can be moved off it by a Dehn twist in the simple horizontal or vertical cylinder whose core curve crosses the saddle connection. We conclude that any periodic point must lie in the orbit of the points marked with circles and hence be a fixed point of the involution. This proves Theorem 5.5 for 𝒬~​(3,−13)\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(3,-1^{3}).

Periodic points in 𝒬⁡(5,−1)\mathcal{Q}(5,-1): Consider the surface on the right in Figure 19. Similarly to the previous case, setting CC to be either of the two middle horizontal cylinders and the 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} to be the two vertical equivalence classes, Lemma 7.1 implies that any periodic point in the union of the two middle horizontal cylinders must be one of the solid dots. Similarly, setting CC to be either of the two middle vertical cylinders and the 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} to be the two horizontal equivalence classes, Lemma 7.1 implies that that any periodic point in the union of the two middle vertical cylinders must be one of the circled points.

The central point of the surface is fixed by the involution and is hence a periodic point; let us exclude this from our discussion. Any other point can be moved to the interior of one of the four cylinders labelled CC in the previous paragraph using Dehn twists. To conclude our analysis of 𝒬~​(5,−1)\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(5,-1) it suffices to show that none of the eight solid or circled points drawn on the surface on the right in Figure 19 are periodic.

By using Dehn twists and symmetry, it suffices to show that the point pp in Figure 20 is not periodic.

In this figure, for any 1>a>01>a>0 the slope 1 direction decomposes into four cylinders. With a=12a=\frac{1}{2}, pp is on the boundary of one of the cylinders, but for nearby aa it is not. By continuity, after changing aa the point pp does not have rational height in the slope 1 cylinder in which it lies, showing that pp is not a periodic point by [Api20, Lemma 5.4]. This proves Theorem 5.5 for 𝒬~​(5,−1)\tilde{\mathcal{Q}}(5,-1).
